subtopic: IMMIGRATION

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I wish to announce specific changes in the immigration regulations, which are being made in the interests of prospective immigrants as
well as Canadian citizens. They will be applied universally and will be non-discriminatory.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN REGULATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The reunification of families remains a fundamental principle of Canadian immigration policy. The government's objective is not to cut back immigration but to moderate the rate of growth.
Mr. Speaker, we Canadians take pride in the fact that we are a nation of immigrants. Even those of us whose families have been in this country for many generations can trace our roots to other lands, other continents. Our nation was built by immigrants and sustained by immigrants. Throughout Canada's history, our national spirit has been continually enriched by new Canadians from other lands. Immigrants opened up this country and pushed back the frontiers. They helped develop Canada as a modern industrial nation. In no small measure they are responsible for our present economic development, our present quality of life.
Canada has always had a strong attraction for people of other parts of the world, and in the last two years this attraction has been growing at an almost unprecedented rate, now accelerating as other countries begin to close down or reduce immigration. The number of people seeking to immigrate to Canada in the first six months of 1974 increased by almost 48 per cent over the substantial level of 1973. Immigrant landings in the same period are 47 per cent more than in the equivalent period in 1973, and 92 per cent more than the same period in 1972. At the present rate, we will land more than 200,000 immigrants in Canada in 1974, and significantly more in the next few years.
But, Mr. Speaker, immigrants are not statistics; they are people. They are people who need jobs, houses, schools and social services. I am announcing changes in our immigration regulations because immigrants are applying for entry and arriving in increasing numbers at a time when employment levels may well be uncertain, when housing is scarce and expensive and many social services are strained to a critical point. These strains are felt particularly in our three major cities where more than one half of the immigrants who arrive this year will settle.
It is important to emphasize that the government must exercise concern for the well-being of prospective immigrants as well as protect our own citizens. It would be irresponsible for the Canadian government to admit more immigrants than we can adequately provide with fundamentals such as jobs, housing and social services. All hon. members are aware that we are working hard on a green paper on immigration. This is a study of population and immigration which will provide the basis for widespread public debate on these topics. It will discuss some of the

October 22, 1974
Immigration
options in these fields available to the government. The green paper will be tabled in this House in the near year, but it will be late in 1975, at the earliest, before new immigration legislation could be expected; and it might be mid-1977 before it would have substantial effects on the immigration flow.
In the interim period, Mr. Speaker, the government has a responsibility to maintain stability in the immigration flow for the reasons I have stated, and so that public debate on new legislation may take place in an ordered and reasonable atmosphere. To provide this stability and lessen the rate of increase in immigrant landings in the months immediately ahead, we are therefore making certain interim changes in the regulations under the present act.
I want to emphasize that the government is taking these steps only after the most careful consideration, and it is taking only those steps which are consistent with the three basic principles of our present immigration policy: first, universality and non-discrimination in the application of selection criteria; second, family reunification; and third, the meeting of Canada's labour market needs.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the House that the following specific changes in the immigration regulations have been approved, effective today, to apply to applications received from this day forward. First, when assessing all independent and nominated applications, the visa officer will in each case, after totalling all the points to which the applicant is entitled under the existing selection system, then determine whether the applicant has satisfactory evidence of bona fide prearranged employment or is going to a designated occupation. In the event that this is not the case, ten points will be deducted from the total achieved.
Second, prospective independent and nominated applicants for immigration to Canada will receive credit under immigration regulations for prearranged employment only when it has been established, normally through a Canada Manpower centre, that no Canadian citizen or permanent resident is available to fill the vacancy. It is more important to note that since at least 50 points are required to gain admission to Canada, independent and nominated immigrants who score 60 points or more would not be affected by these changes. These adjustments take into account the natural concern of permanent residents in Canada about job opportunities. They are also designed to protect immigrants themselves who might otherwise have great difficulty finding jobs, housing or access to social services.
I want to emphasize that the changes I have just outlined do not-I repeat, do not-apply to sponsored immigrants, that is, to close relatives of Canadians or of landed immigrants. These close relatives will continue to come to Canada under the same conditions that have been in force for several years. The new regulations will apply in exactly the same manner to both the other categories, the independent and nominated immigrants, no matter where they were born or at what post they submit their applications. Again I emphasize that the changes will affect applications received from today forward, but not those already on hand. In other words, they are not going to apply retroactively.
(Mr. Andras.]
The new regulations will have no impact on Canada's traditional concern for, and response to, the persecuted and the displaced. We will continue to deal compassionately with refugees, victims of oppression or cases where other humanitarian considerations apply. Also, the new regulations will not prevent employers with a genuine need for labour which is unavailable in Canada from selecting immigrants to meet their needs. Indeed, when conditions warrant, this action will enhance our ability and we will take steps to help speed the entry of workers destined to employers whose requirements are particularly pressing.
Hon. members are well aware of the government's concern about the level of Francophone immigration to Canada. While immigrants from all countries will be affected by the changes, I want to stress our resolve to continue to encourage the flow of Francophone immigrants to Canada within the constraints established by the new regulations.
The changes that I have announced represent the fairest, the most just and, I think, the most equitable measures that we could find to deal with the anticipated increased flow of immigrants to Canada in the months ahead; and they are far less sweeping and more satisfactory than those changes we would be forced to contemplate a year or two from now if we did not act today.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to thank the minister for making his statement available to me well in advance of the sitting of the House today. Having had statements respecting changing the regulations from both the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the minister-not only in the House but outside- during the last week or ten days, the minister's statement today came as no surprise. In my opinion, the minister's statement is a reflex action to a much larger problem than that to which the minister is giving credence. The problem is: what type of immigration and population policy will Canadians have in the 1970s and onward as we look at future growth in Canada?
From our point of view this statement is one of absolute confusion. The minister said early in his statement, "The government's objective is not to cut back immigration but to moderate the rate of growth." Through you, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the minister what that statement means. First, he does not want to cut back immigration but he wants to cut back the rate of immigration.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN REGULATIONS
speechtext: No. The rate of growth.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN REGULATIONS
speechtext:
All right, the rate of growth. But that and the immigration rate is the same thing. I agree with the minister when he points out the desirability of Canada as a potential area for immigrants, especially in light of the present situation when many countries of the industrialized world are closing their borders to immigrants, specifically New Zealand and Australia. However, the statement again points out that the government still accepts the so-called TAP policy on immigration. That is a policy which ties the volume of immigration supposedly to job openings or to the rising unemployment rate. That means that as unemployment increases, we reduce the rate of
October 22, 1974

immigration; and as unemployment drops, we increase the rate of immigration.
To me, this statement clearly indicates that this government fears the winter of 1974-75 because a rise in the rate of unemployment will mean a cutback on immigration as jobs will not be available. That is what the government is saying in this statement. This is a knee-jerk reaction to something the government desperately fears. It just does not know which way to move.
We must keep in mind that immigrants not only take jobs and are workers; they are also consumers and they stimulate the economy. There must be a fine balance between the number of jobs we want to make available to immigrants and the number of jobs they actually create. Furthermore, the statement cler-rly points out that the government is still plodding along-and will do so up to 1977, for the matter-hopefully legislating by regulation. I would ask again, where is the green paper? We have reason to believe that it can be presented in the very near future. Surely the expression of Canadians regarding future population growth as indicated in the briefs presented when the green paper was compiled should be related to the demand and the need for future Canadian immigration policy.
The government says it is now going to bring in another regulation while the green paper is in the process of being developed. I suggest this is just another reaction to the problem. Clearly, what we need is a balanced immigration policy. This immigration policy for Canada, to my mind, is geared to the centralist view, that is, the general view of the industrialized areas of Ontario and Quebec. As unemployment increases in those areas, you reduce immigration.
Let me point out-I am sure the minister is aware of this-that there are other regions of this country which desperately need workers, particularly western and northern Canada. We have been able to fill some of these job vacancies only with immigrants who were willing to take them and apparently Canadians did not want the jobs. While restricting regulations are necessary and are dictated by areas of unemployment, there are other areas of Canada which need workers to hammer nails, to lay floors and to work in stores. We need workers in Alberta and in northern Canada. Is the minister now saying that we are to have a complete reduction in immigration? Is he suggesting that although there are jobs available in some areas, we are to have a universal restriction and reduction? I say this is a policy which must take regional factors into consideration very definitely. In respect of the regulations the minister has brought in he has tied them to an extent to job openings.

speechtext:
Thank you for your indulgence, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion I should like to suggest to the minister that the regulations he has brought in today have already been in operation in various immigration offices across the world. He says, not directly. I believe there are very direct practical implications to that. Further, I should like to suggest that the minister should give us more clarification in respect of these regulations. For instance, how long have these regulations which he announced today been in the offices.
My last point is a sensitive matter relating specifically to Francophone immigration. I feel the minister has merely touched this sensitive area, and I should like him to explain in much greater detail whether or not the ten points will be deducted if Francophone immigration is encouraged. Will the ten points be deducted if no jobs are available?
The statement points out that changes in the 1952 and subsequent regulations are necessary. I hope the minister will take to heart that what is needed is a comprehensive program and not simply the amendment of regulations from time to time in respect of a problem which already exists.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are some things in the statement of the minister with which we wholeheartedly agree and which we welcome. The first is that family reunification, as a basis for immigration policy, remains the same as before. This is as it should be. We also welcome the fact that the new regulations will not have a negative impact with regard to Canada's concern for refugees, the persecuted and the displaced. However, we believe that instead of the problems of refugees being dealt with on an ad hoc basis as each emergency arises, regulations or legislation should be prepared specifically setting out conditions on which refugees may be admitted to Canada.
We, of course, agree with the minister that immigration must depend upon opportunities for employment, housing and social services in Canada. But it is because of the failure of the government to provide adequate and full employment policies and the failure of the government's economic policies that we are now having to consider the restriction of the flow of immigrants into Canada.
No one will deny that the immigrants coming into Canada have been responsible for the growth of this country, for the variety of cultures that have enriched Canada and which have conferred many benefits on Canada. But we must seek an expanding economy in which the great resources of Canada can be used to accommodate an increased flow of immigrants, and in which restrictive measures can be removed.
We find it rather odd to learn that the government is making such a fanfare about these new immigration regulations. The fact of the matter is that on February 21, 1974, by P.C.318 of 1974, regulations were made which restricted immigration of independent applicants and of nominated relatives to those who had arranged definite employment in Canada with reasonable prospects of continuity in meeting local conditions of work and wages or where

October 22, 1974
Motion-Mr. Andras
there was occupational demand. The new regulations do not seem so very different. The mountains have laboured and have produced a mouse.
Of course, we welcome the minister's assurance that universality and nondiscrimination is a basic principle of our present immigration policy. We trust that under no circumstances will any Canadian government be tempted to depart from this policy. Indeed, we would like to see it applied more realistically by making the immigration facilities available on a more even basis throughout the world.
Lastly, we note that the government is working hard on a green paper on immigration but that we need not expect the immigration legislation until 1975. We wonder if even that is a serious deadline. There have been no substantial amendments to the Immigration Act since it was passed some time in the 1940's. In 1966, the government published a white paper which proposed numerous changes in obsolete sections of the Immigration Act. The minister then was the present Minister of Transport. This was supposed to be the prelude to early legislative action. It is now six years later and it looks as though we shall not get any amendments to the Immigration Act until approximately ten years after this official document setting out policy was produced.
However, perhaps it would be less than generous not to admit that if the present minister, unlike most of his predecessors, stays on the job and lives up to the promises made, we may at last have a new and more up to date Immigration Act, if not in 1975, perhaps in 1977.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON CHANGES IN REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the statement of the hon. Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) and I noted that it contained some good points. Among other things, the reunion of families remains one of the basic principles of the Canadian immigration policy. We agree completely on this point. We understand that there can be special circumstances, and on the basis mostly of humanitarian principles, we want to help people in difficult situations.
The minister also said that immigrants have opened this country and pushed the frontiers back. We also agree about this, since reports on immigration at various periods show that less than 350 years ago, the first European settler, Louis Hebert, arrived at the Quebec City trading post. He was later followed by immigrants of various nationalities. However, we should control closely the arrival in Canada, under favorable circumstances, of selected immigrants. There are standards to be met if we do not want to get undesirables.
Advertising must also be controlled closely and overly attractive propaganda which often prepares the immigrant to more hardships than success must be curtailed if necessary. Seeing publicity pamphlets showing Canada as an overly promising country, foreigners often decide to immigrate to Canada and find themselves unemployed a few months later. This is unfair both to the unemployed Canadians and to the immigrants who cannot find employment. All appropriate efforts should be made in order to establish the necessary contacts between employ-

ers and employees, to ensure that our available manpower can find desirable jobs, before thinking of expanding various immigration programs.
I know it is not always easy to find the right solution to the many problems in the field of manpower, but it should be much easier to come to an agreement with our own citizens by allowing our young people to get some experience, even in temporary jobs, despite the fact that employers require, and rightly so, experienced people in the jobs they have to offer.
Accordingly, if we counsel our young people and all those who want to work in Canada, we would accommodate the employers; I feel that we should limit immigration at least until such time as the unemployment situation has stabilized in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. A study conducted by the University of Guelph, the results of which were released by the CBC last Sunday, showed that of 108 samples of ground-beef taken from 28 supermarkets representing the major chains, 46 per cent contained staphylococci bacteria that are dangerous and capable of causing food poisoning. Therefore I should like to move;
That the government give immediate consideration to implementing the recommendations contained in the Food Prices Review Board report on ground-beef released on June 6th, 1974.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER RECOMMENDATIONS IN FINKELMAN REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first to say to the minister that the matter he has just raised in the House concerning this joint committee is most welcome. I was also pleased to hear his statement concerning the Public Service Superannuation Act and the fact that the committee may also have an opportunity to study that legislation. I think such a study, and indeed a study of the whole position of the public service vis-a-vis bargaining, is long overdue. I fully realize that an election intervened, but the minister may recall that from time to time during the twenty-ninth parliament I raised the question of when these matters would be brought forward for consideration.
At the outset I wish to pay tribute to the chairman, Mr. Finkelman, who in his own right is a very distinguished public servant. I would not want any remarks I make with regard to this matter in any way to indicate that I have anything other than the highest regard for his services to Canada and to the public generally. He was given a large mandate by the government of Canada, namely, to examine the Public Service Staff Relations Act and its administration and to make recommendations on how it could be amended or revised in order adequately to meet the needs of employers and employees in the public service and the employee organizations. Then last, but certainly not least in importance, Mr. Finkelman's recommendations were to deal with how the public service could best serve the interests of the public at large.
Many public servants have felt for some time that the system is not operating as it should and that it can, and should, operate much better. Many public servants have spoken to me and other members of parliament about the greatest difficulty which seems to confront them, that is, the fact that either directly or indirectly many of them suffer from the impersonality of the operation. I suppose that is a disease that results from bigness. There is lack of positive connection between the work that people do and the result of that work, in action or policy, and if anything that is an irritant to the disease.
Public servants say in their own way that the impersonal, bureaucratic operation denies them the ultimate human satisfaction from work-the feeling of participation, of fulfilment, and in some cases of a sense of importance and the completeness of their task. I realize that these are matters which cannot be legislated but they can be affected by conditions of work and particularly by the relationship between employers and employees. If this is the case, I believe it will be the task of the committee to look at the public service, not just from the point of view of the government and of the public-though they are important-also from the point of view of the public servant himself, or herself. If this important aspect is not forgotten, then I believe the public interest will in fact be served by the committee's investigation and the matters which will flow from it.
I respectfully suggest it is also important that we do not approach this study with any preconceived notions based on any outdated concept rooted in antiquity but, rather, with an openness of mind, bearing in mind that the whole question of employer-employee relations is a dynamic thing that is changing more rapidly, day by day, than ever before.
606

There are needs to be fulfilled on each side of the bargaining table, and there is a public interest that may not necessarily be embodied completely in the interests of either side. The importance of the maintenance of a public service with a sense of dedication and purpose is increasing, particularly in view of the continued and growing incidence of intervention of government into the lives of people. The federal public service is in many ways a model for the public services of other jurisdictions inside and outside this country, as are its individual members, and the contribution of the public service itself in many fields of endeavour is important to this country and all its people. There are many in the public service who have resolved to serve for less remuneration than they could have obtained elsewhere, because they believe that their work is important.
It is not possible, nor is it proper, for me at this point to review each of the 231 recommendations of the Finkelman report. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that it relieves you considerably to hear me say that. But I think it is essential that the general approach of the parties to be represented on the committee should be laid out before the House before consideration of the report by the committee. I regret very much that the government did not see fit to do that in the statement made by the House leader today.
In general terms, with some notable and unfortunate exceptions, progress to date under the existing collective bargaining procedures has been good. Subject to those exceptions, there have been improvements in the number of agreements being reached and in the period of time that elapses between the beginning of negotiations and the reaching of the agreement. At first there was hesitancy in government generally to expand bargaining rights and whatever expansions there were some six years ago were somewhat limited because, I suppose, of novelty, apprehension, or perhaps a bit of both. I think it is fair to say- with all the wisdom of hindsight, I must admit-that the government could have gone much further than it did a few years ago.
We believe that the experience gained to date by both Treasury Board and the staff associations more than justifies the claim that the time has come to take a hard look at the exclusions contained in the present act, the area of job security, standards of classification, check-off, grievance procedures, transfers, retirement, leave, and a host of other areas. These should be reviewed and serious consideration given to lifting the exclusions. I mean no disrespect to Mr. Finkelman when I suggest that perhaps his approach to these matters is somewhat conservative, with a small "c". Normally I do not mean a small "c" when I use that word. Perhaps it is the way in which a person in his position should approach the matter, but conservative it is and it is the duty of the committee to listen to both sides, and also to Mr. Finkelman, to plumb their points of view and to make recommendations to this House.
If I may comment on the report itself, it seems to presume that there is some immaturity which we, for our part, do not believe exists. We believe there is an understanding respecting the responsibility of Treasury Board, on one hand, and staff associations on the other, that neither will act by their nature outside the public interest,

that each will try to do what is right, and that the ability to collectively bargain, negotiate and arbitrate should be set over the widest range of subject matter. If that happens, the attitude of confidence and trust of the employees in the system will be fostered and strengthened, and the collective bargaining procedures will be strengthened as well by an open approach. We believe that this strengthening is important to what I might call industrial peace or peace between employers and employees in the public service.
There is another fundamental area to which I should like to turn at this time; that is, the vexing and difficult problem of persons employed in managerial or confidential capacities and the exclusion of many of these people from the bargaining unit. As Mr. Finkelman himself said at page 29 of volume I of the report, the problem is in drawing the line and it is a very difficult problem indeed. We will have to examine the report in detail, as well as the present law, but it seems to me-and I respectfully submit this to the House-that the committee should approach the question from the point of view that the benefits and burdens of participation in the collective bargaining process should be available to as broad a range of public servants as possible.
Moreover, it should be approached from the point of view that the public servant can, in fact, separate his personal interest from his responsibilities to the employer, rather than from the point of view that he cannot do so. As well, there should be trusted machinery to make the determination when this is necessary. It is from that point of view-what I would call a positive point of view-that I said a careful examination of the definitions proposed on pages 39, 40 and 41 of volume I should be undertaken.
The last point with which I wish to deal is the resolution of public interest disputes and the right to strike. I commend to all members the text on pages 121 to 125 where this right is examined and the difficulty of removing it is set forth in simple and direct terms. It is stated in the report that the best way of resolving an impasse is to prevent it from arising. But this sage saying, coupled with the words of Mr. Finkelman, does not allow a government to wash its hands of responsibility to protect the public interest. The public is the third party at the bargaining table.
A review of 1973 and 1974, even by a most impartial observer, will indicate that the government's attitude toward this public responsibility has been unfortunate, to say the least. It is a period in which there has been a general deterioration in the attitude that should exist between employers and employees. A few days ago we heard in this House the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) indicate how belatedly the government had come to the conclusion that machinery must be established to review the question of the public interest and its protection.
In the private sector, we have advocated the establishment of a public interest disputes commission, pursuant to the recommendations of the Woods report, with responsibility for determining and defining the absolutely essential aspects of services coming under federal jurisdiction, the provision of which should not be grossly interfered with due to a breakdown in collective bargaining. The intent is to provide all possible assistance to facilitate the
October 22, 1974

conclusion of agreements but, if necessary, to assist in alleviating damage that may occur and to report to the minister from time to time and make recommendations as to what steps, if any, should be taken with respect to any particular matter.
I have read Mr. Finkelman's observations regarding the right to strike and the right to lock out, as well as his recommendations as to the timing and the steps that should be taken leading to settlement. It is my hope that by reason of the improvements the committee will make, the vast majority of bargaining will lead to successful settlements and the public interest will be protected in that way. At the same time, it should not be beyond the purview of the committee to review what is an essential service in the public sector or to suggest the establishment of machinery to make that review. It should make recommendations to this House based on its findings, bearing in mind the rights of participants in the collective bargaining process.
I wish to make it clear that my party does not believe that rights which have been granted ought lightly to be taken away. We respectfully point out that if government intervention in the community grows, the withdrawal of essential services will have greater and greater impact. That being so, I think the committee ought to consider what is an essential service. As I said at the outset, we welcome the formation of this committee and look forward to participating in its work.
I began my speech by saying we are concerned about the position of the public servant as an individual and not a mere cog in the bureaucratic machine. The committee, in its considerations, should not forget that important element. While the talk is great and important, if we build up a reservoir of trust so that we can make the public service a good place of work for men and women of Canada, the public interest will be served. I hope the work of the committee will develop that relationship of trust which is so necessary if this work is to be successfully carried out.

Mr. Speaker, we welcome the decision to establish a special parliamentary committee to consider the Finkelman report. Like the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), I shall begin by making my first comment one that relates to the last item, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) mentioned in presenting this motion. We welcome warmly the word that consideration is being given to amending the Public Service Superannuation Act. I look forward to the possibility of seeing the subject dealt with by the same special committee. The last time the whole question of collective bargaining in the public service was dealt with by a special committee, that same special committee had before it matters relating to the Public Service Superannuation Act. It is good to be back again at both of these subjects.
There is no gainsaying that public service pension arrangements in Canada are good, and we have won important improvements. But there are serious shortcomings. There are things which definitely need to be improved. If I am not careful, I will be launching out into my full-dress speech on this subject, but that would
Public Service
hardly be appropriate at this time. I simply say that we welcome the fact that this subject as well as the material in the Finkelman report, will in due course be referred to this special committee.
With regard to the Public Service Staff Relations Act, I underline the very fine sentiments which have been expressed by my friend from Grenville-Carleton, who emphasized that it is important for workers of any category, and especially workers who are serving the public, to have a sense of participating in what they are doing. That is what collective bargaining is all about. As my late friend Andy Andras used to say, the purpose of collective bargaining is to turn a hand into a man. This is what the labour movement has been seeking across the years, the recognition that those who toil are not just cogs in a machine, but human beings with rights and aspirations which deserve to be respected.
I was happy to be the member of the committee which considered the Public Service Staff Relations Act in the first place, in other words, the committee which first recommended back to parliament the entire set-up with respect to collective bargaining. I am pleased that we shall have this opportunity to review the whole matter.
As has already been said, despite the shortcomings- especially the interminable delays-the over-all experience with collective bargaining in the public service has been good. No one is suggesting that we drop it. But there are certain improvements which need to be made. I am glad that we have the advice of Mr. Finkelman in his report, which we shall consider in committee. As the previous speaker said, Mr. Finkelman made 231 recommendations, so that if every speaker in this debate were to deal with them seriatim we should never get around to the competition bill which is on the agenda for today.
Let me refer to one or two of Mr. Finkelman's recommendations. I like his general suggestion that the Public Service Staff Relations Act should be made as much like the Canada Labour Code as possible. There are differences between employment in the private sector and employment in the public service. But I think those differences should not be treated in a way which is to the disadvantage of those in the public service. I suggest, as Mr. Finkelman has, that there are practices sanctioned by the Canada Labour Code which might well be imported into the Public Service Staff Relations Act.
With respect to one of the other questions to which the previous speaker referred, that of the exclusion of certain subjects from collective bargaining, I regret that Mr. Finkelman has been a bit conservative-and I am not sure that is spelled with a small "c"-in recommending no significant changes. Although he does recommend a strengthening of the consultation process with regard to these various areas, it is still my view and the view of my colleagues that things such as classification, job security and promotion should be the subject of collective bargaining. When we get the Finkelman report to the committee we will have these issues before us and we can deal with them there.
Likewise, I am a bit disappointed that the Finkelman report does not treat in what I call a democratic fashion the matter of excluded employees. I am now distinguishing employees from subjects. There are already too many

excluded subjects. I suggest that, likewise, there are too many excluded employees, even if Mr. Finkelman comes up with suggestions as to ways in which there might be more active consultation regarding their position. He also proposes that there be a better method of defining and designating those who are not to be covered by collective bargaining. So, without spelling it out, I think I have said enough to emphasize that there are these problems to deal with and that they will be before us once this report is in the hands of the special committee.
There are two or three matters that are not the subject of recommendations in the report but which I think are important. I said earlier that the collective bargaining process in the public service has gone well, except for a few shortcomings, one being the time loss that occurs in many negotiations. Whether that is the fault of the legislation or the fault of the government is, of course, a point about which one can argue. I certainly think it would be a tremendous boon to the health of the collective bargaining process if we could take steps to speed it up as far as the public service is concerned.
Another matter which may not lend itself so much to the legislation as to the whole question of public policy is to be found in the fact that the government seems to be able to make very low offers of wage and salary increases to those involved in the collective bargaining process- perhaps only 2 per cent or even 7 per cent per year. When it comes to senior officials such as deputy ministers, however, in the second or third grade, or even the top ones, there is a tremendous boost. Salaries of $45,000, $55,000, or even more, are not the result of collective bargaining but of a process outside it altogether. It raises the whole question of the fairness and morality of percentage wage and salary adjustments when those at the lower level get such low increases, in terms of actual dollars, compared with those at a higher level.
There is another area where high salaries are paid and it has been suggested today that there might be a discussion on increasing them as well. I am not going to raise that matter now, except to say that I take the same view, namely, that our concern in this place should not be for those of us who are not suffering any distress, but it should be for those in the lower brackets. What I am saying with respect to the public service is that even if it is necessary to have some employees outside the collective bargaining process, the government must do a better job of rationalizing what it does for those on higher salaries compared with what it does for those covered by collective bargaining.
I noted the comments made by the previous speaker about the proposals of his party for a public interest disputes commission. I can go along with him and all the other "after dinner" speakers who say that we should try to find a better way than strikes to solve labour disputes. Every labour leader in the country is prepared to endorse that proposition. There should be a better way. What I object to is the suggestion that labour must give up the right to strike before that better way has been found. I commend those who try to find a better way. I have spent some time and thought on it myself. But none of us has yet found it, and I do not think any derogatory remarks

should be made about labour, whether in the private sector or in the public service, using the only weapon available to them to try to improve their position.
I like the comment of my hon. friend from Grenville-Carleton who suggested that what has been given to the public service as a right should not be lightly taken away. I would amend the statement and take out the word "lightly". It has been given to them and it should not be taken away. This involves the whole question of an economy that functions properly. In this parliament we are "at" the government on this question every day. But I suggest if the economy is not functioning properly, we should not take it out on particular groups of people and, in particular, we should not take it out on the public service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make a lengthy intervention today. I listened with great interest to the speeches of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). May I express my thanks through you, sir, to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for his kind remarks about my speech of October 10 in the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
Those of us who are concerned about the public service have been looking forward to the creation of this type of committee. There is a real job to be done. When I spoke on the matter in the throne speech debate, I expressed concern because of the difficulties of collective bargaining in the public service. We have a serious problem of price movement and inflation. Without question, awards have not kept up with the movement of prices in the general economy. Many of the contracts arrived at by the staff associations have led to a great deal of discontent.
I expressed concern then about the numbers who had taken the strike option, and I expressed the hope that the government would move promptly to establish the committee which is the subject of the motion before us. I think the speeches of the two hon. members who preceded me in this debate are a good omen-because they sit on the other side of the House-in terms of the measure of agreement which will probably exist in the committee. They did not take a partisan approach; they took a moderate and sympathetic attitude to the general problems of the public service. I share the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as to the scope of the committee's work. I hope the committee will be able to consider, not only the Public Service Staff Relations Act and the superannuation act but a number of other matters.
I have been concerned not only about the administration of the public service-and I do not intend to repeat the observations I made on that subject-but about lack of mobility in the service, lack of a policy on transfers, lack of opportunity which would allow employees who have been on the job for a long time to meet a new challenge and get a new start. Those of us who follow public service affairs recall that not long ago positions were filled through a process of widely advertised competitions conducted by duly constituted boards which published the results of their decisions. This was the general practice. Then came technological innovation, Datastream-the great big computer.
Those of us who have listened to complaints from public servants affected must be concerned about the operations of this computer system since there are side effects which are less than desirable. Nowadays there is often no competition in the normal sense. A request is made by a departmental head, authority is delegated, a computer search takes place and half an hour later some cards are pulled out, the top names are interviewed and the placement is
Combines Investigation Act
made. In many ways the procedure is perhaps more efficient than former methods, but employees who are seeking a new challenge, who realize they have gone as far as they can in the jobs they hold, often do not have an opportunity to appear before a selection board. One cannot help feeling there is a group of people who specialize in the writing of computer cards. If all the key words appear on the computer card in the right places, that card is most likely to be pulled out in the event of a search and opportunities will flow.
I am reminded of the specialists who have developed in applying for LIP grants. Let us face it, there are people who have learned to write a strong submission. That is their specialty. The content of their submission may not be as good as its form, but nevertheless it attracts something better than the average hearing. I feel there is a somewhat similar procedure undertaken with respect to computer operation data streams. There are some who manage to have good cards written, the key words are all in the correct places, and they enjoy much better opportunities than others who must employ more pedestrian methods of coping with a mechanized operation.
I do not know to what extent the committee will be able to discuss such matters as this. However, I am certainly of the opinion that the question of transfers and promotions-matters which in any large corporation are generally handled by a personnel department-should be examined by the committee.
I join other hon. members in saying that the general recommendations made by Mr. Finkelman are small "c" conservative. I hope there will be general agreement among the members of the committee to come forward with at least a degree of unanimity so that legislation can proceed very quickly. However, I trust we shall also take the opportunity to consider a number of broader questions. I was interested in the suggestions put forward by the speakers who preceded me, and I certainly have an open mind on what they said.
Motion agreed to.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to move that Bill C-2 be read the second time. As you know, it is the third time that this bill is brought forward in this House and this is the second debate on second reading. The Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs had made a lot of progress in the study of this bill when Parliament was dissolved last May for the general election. I therefore

October 22, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
hope that all hon. members will take these facts into account during this debate and will try to speed up consideration of this bill, at least on second reading.
As I have already mentioned, Bill C-2 is the same as Bill C-227 brought forward on November 5, 1973, and Bill C-7, introduced in the House of Commons on February 28,1974. Since that time, our position on some aspects of the bill has been modified to take into account the reaction of the public to the previous bills.
I plan to suggest amendments to the bill when it is studied in committee. In my opinion, there is nothing mysterious in this, and we do not intend to suggest any mysterious amendment. My predecessor had already told the members of the parliamentary committee about the contents of most of these amendments. They have been circulated amongst the members of this committee and are well known. I will present them again during the study in committee.
Almost all the amendments were the result of extremely useful and constructive briefs or suggestions that were presented to the parliamentary committee by various groups, or came from officials in my department following a more careful study of that bill and of the effects of some aspects of it.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, is the result of five years of intensive discussions with representatives from various sectors of the populations, not to mention the years of studies devoted to it by the Economic Council of Canada, in order to analyze the competition policy Canada needs to face the problems of today and the challenges of tomorrow.
It was in 1966 that the government asked the Economic Council of Canada to study the three spheres of action now under the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and to make recommendations. Those three spheres of action are: first, consumer affairs, second, the competition policy and third, the laws concerning intellectual property.
The Council made a report on each of those spheres of action and the three reports have greatly influenced the government's as well as the Canadian public's outlook. The report made by the Economic Council of Canada on the competition policy was presented to the government during the summer of 1969. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs of that time, the present member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Basford), immediately created a committee of experts to guide him in the implementation of the Council's recommendations. He also asked people from all sectors to examine the report and give them their views on it.
In June 1971, when the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs introduced Bill C-256, he insisted upon the fact that the object of the bill was to invite discussion rather than result in an immediate implementation. I will remind you that we are in 1974. I think that the wishes of the minister at that time have indeed been carried out. It is unquestionable that this bill has been the subject of much discussion and that all of its aspects have been carefully examined. I would not want to encroach upon the wishes of the minister when I say that when he

thought this bill should be discussed rather than immediately voted on, he surely did not have in mind a date later than this time in 1974.
I think one of the important tasks in the elaboration of this bill for Parliament was accomplished by my predecessor, the present hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), who recommended to the government the various steps to be followed in setting up a competition policy. In doing so, he received the help of the Special Committee of the House of Commons on Trends in Food Prices. That committee which was set up, as hon. members will recall, in January of 1973 clearly understood the urgent need to reform the competition legislation, but it also realized that some aspects of the competition policy such as corporate mergers could not be amended too quickly and that they should rather be examined in terms of their integration into other government industrial measures. The committee recommended to the government that it legislate instead on certain aspects of the competition policy which did not pose the same difficulties, especially in the area of consumer protection.
So Bill C-227 introduced before this House by my predecessor, the hon. member for Windsor West, in November of 1973 reflected the views of the committee in that it did not touch on certain aspects of the competition policy such as corporate mergers, monopolistic situations and specialization agreements.
In his speech on the second reading of Bill C-7 which was identical to this bill, Mr. Speaker, the then minister made a lengthy description of the contents of that bill. I think this House would be better served if I dispensed with repeating all those technical details. However, I think it would be useful for members interested in this bill to read over that speech which can be found in the Hansard of March 13, 1974. It was an excellent speech that I urge everyone to read because it reflects the quality and the competence of the man who made it and to whom I would want to pay a particular tribute for his never-ending dedication and his remarkable relentlessness in working for Canadian consumers and small businessmen.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I would like particularly to bring out the highlights and the reasons for our action, stressing particularly some of the main amendments to the Combines Investigation Act contained in this bill.
First, there is a series of prohibitions concerning specific business practices that are detrimental to the consumer. Those provisions create criminal offenses or being about desirable amendments to existing prohibitions.
In the first place, provisions concerning misleading advertising are revised and made more accurate so that they apply to false statements of every kind made to the public about products or services rather than to advertisements only. Not only the literal meaning of the statements will be taken into account, but also the general impression that they give. Then, false or fraudulent warranties and testimonials are prohibited.
Furthermore, any sale at a price other that the lowest of two or more prices is prohibited in the case of double ticketed products.
October 22, 1974

Also, pyramid selling is prohibited under certain reservations as well as referral selling according to their definition.
Bait and switch selling is also prohibited.
Selling above advertised price is also prohibited.
Promotional contests are prohibited except when they comply with regulations.
Finally, the price fixing prohibition is reinforced.
A series of amendments will, on application by the director of investigation and research authorize the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission first, to examine cases of refusal to sell and after the supplier has been given every opportunity to be heard, to order him to supply his customers to recommend price changes; second, to examine cases of consignment selling to control the prices of a supplier or establish price differences between competitors and after the supplier has been given every opportunity to be heard, to order him to cease this practice.
Third, to examine cases of exclusivity where some big suppliers demand of their buyers that they sell some particular products only to reduce competition and, after the suppliers has been given reasonable opportunity to be heard, to make the appropriate remedial order.
Fourth, to study cases when tied selling, that is the practice whereby the selling of a product is tied to the selling of another one, is being practised by major suppliers, in order to substantially lessen competition in the market, and after having given suppliers a fair hearing, to make the appropriate remedial order.
Fifth, to study cases when market restrictions, that is the fact that a supplier of a product, as a condition of supplying the product to a customer, requires him to supply the product in a specific market only, is also being practised by major suppliers in order to substantially lessen competition in the market, and once again, after having given suppliers a fair hearing, to make the appropriate remedial order.
Sixth, and last, to study cases when foreign judgments, foreign laws or instructions from foreign directors are detrimental to the Canadian public interest and, after having given them a fair hearing, to make orders prohibiting their application in Canada.
Another aspect of those amendments relates to the prohibitions of the Act dealing with combinations, mergers and monopolies that are now restricted mainly to the production and trade of items and goods. Those prohibitions have a broader scope, and apply now to all services and service industries.
I would also like to deal with the provisions designed to allow and facilitate civil actions for the purpose of recovering losses or damages resulting from an offence to the law, up to the extent of the total sum, plus enquiry and prosecution costs.
Mr. Speaker, I see that my time is running short and I obviously cannot discuss every aspect of the bill. I shall of course have the occasion to do so in greater detail during the clause by clause examination of the bill in committee.
Combines Investigation Act
Mr. Speaker, earlier in my remarks, I stressed the fact that Bill C-2 stems from a most thorough and detailed analysis led by the government and the general public. I should like to revert to that remark, because I believe it is essential and I hope that all members of this House will understand that we have already examined this bill long enough. We have tried to answer criticism whenever we could without going against the fundamental principles of a competition policy. This compromise process is not over and I have no hesitation in saying so. I am convinced that this process will be continued during the discussion in committee with the advice that the members from this and the other side of the House will be giving. I am open to any constructive suggestion that may be brought forth.
However, I will say this, Mr. Speaker. Despite all our efforts I am the first one to say, and I am sure that the other members of this House will agree with me, that it is impossible to satisfy everyone, especially in this field. No one is in favour of the implementation of policies which will hinder his freedom. To be efficient, this bill must restrict the liberty of action of powerful concerns more than the present Combines Investigation Act. It is obvious that this causes certain problems. It causes some annoyance. But I think it is essential, for if we were to satisfy all our critics, I think in the end we would adopt legislation that would be even weaker than the present law.
Much criticism coming from businessmen where we could not reach a compromise concerns the proposal of making some trade practices subject to review by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. It has even been suggested that the present bill gives unlimited discretionary powers to the Commission to control business.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the small number of practices subject to review by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission are carefully defined in this bill. There is no need to make loud protests and to suggest that this legislation will give unlimited power in this case. There is no need to exaggerate the scope and the powers given to the Commission.
The situation is the same for the required conditions for the Commission to be authorized to issue an order dealing with these restrictive practices. Moreover, it is mentioned in the bill that the concerned parties must be given the opportunity to be heard and that is a very good opportunity for them to put forward their views completely. And I repeat that the federal court's Act provides for appeals on interpretation issues. So any party who may feel that the Commission is given too much power could come before it and appeal against the ruling of the Commission.
Mr. Speaker, may I say that we are prepared to make any other arrangement we deem warranted to meet critics. The purpose of some of the amendments which I referred to in the beginning of my speech is to clarify the discretionary powers granted to the Commission. But there is a basic principle which we can depart from. In part, we must go from a criminal law to a civil law to face some trade practices which are currently widespread. Those are desirable and justified in some cases, I must say. Those are not practices which may be considered as bad at first glance. However, in other circumstances, the same practices could be prejudicial to competition. It is simply impossible to eliminate those sort of practices with a

October 22, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
criminal law. We cannot meet the critics in that field. This would jeopardize the integrity of this bill and somewhat sabotage Phase II of our competition policy which has yet to be introduced. Mr. Speaker, although I may sometimes appear eager for compromise, this time I have no intention to come to an arrangement.
On the other hand, I am sure that most Canadian businessmen realize that it is in their best interest in the long run to support responsible legislation such as Bill C-2, for this will provide a strong competition policy. After all, is it not our purpose to foster a sound and progressive free enterprise system? No one would benefit if we were to allow a minority group to use restrictive and anti-social practices which would throw discredit over the private system as we know it now.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I will not hide the fact that I consider all Canadian consumers as my own constituents. I feel that consumers and businessmen have an interest in common, that is, a market where prices are set by the interaction of competitive forces and where honesty and fair play prevail. I agree that Bill C-2 contains the fewest possible limitations on private enterprise which are compatible with the need to safeguard consumers interests as well as those of these same businessmen when purchasing goods and services.
I could never bring myself to introduce a bill which could be detrimental to the interests of such important people as our businessmen. If I am firmly convinced that this bill will not prejudice the legitimate interests and expectations of Canadian businessmen, I am not less convinced that this necessary and long awaited bill will prove infinitely important not only to all Canadian consumers, but even more so to the small Canadian businessman.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, probably no one in this House would quarrel with the principle of Bill C-2. Certainly, my caucus endorses the concept of open competition, with proper safeguards for the consumer and the prevention of abusive business practices. Expressed another way, surely no member of this House would advocate conspiracies to fix prices or would endorse pyramid selling, referral selling, misleading advertising or double-ticketing.
That is not the question here. What is of importance here is: will this bill, in its present form, contribute to better competition in this country? Will this bill, with its amendments to existing legislation, improve that legislation so that improper business activities will no longer exist or will at least lessen in this country? In short, will it be an improvement on present legislation now available to the courts and to the Canadian public? Finally, in considering Bill C-2, in all fairness we must also look at the Trudeau government's record in respect of the consumers in this country, and in particular at that government's record in respect of lessening or containing rising prices.
Unfortunately, the government's handling of consumer protection, and therefore the formation of a new competition policy in Canada, has been most inadequate. Bill C-2, if passed in its present form, may be little more than a

hoax on the Canadian public. Rather than lower prices, the effect of its implementation may well be to raise prices in Canada. The government appears to be so unsure of its position that even now we hear the minister state that he intends to amend the bill which is before us when it reaches the committee. Why cannot we have the amendments on the floor of the House at this time? Surely it is an affront to this parliament to suggest that some amendments which were put before a committee a few months ago are those which everybody in this House should assume the minister has in mind when he says the bill will be amended. I would strongly recommend that the minister quit playing games. If he knows exactly what form the new legislation should take, then he should produce the amendments and let the members of this House see the true impact he has in mind for Bill C-2.
Let us quickly trace the record of this government, as the minister has already done, with regard to this type of legislation. In one parliament the government introduced Bill C-256, which received such adverse comment from the business community and many other quarters, consumers included, that it was allowed to die. The government then proposed through a stage one and a stage two approach to attain, presumably, a similar objective. Stage one, which was Bill C-227, appeared in November, 1973, during the first session of the twenty-ninth parliament, and reappeared as Bill C-7 in the last session of the last parliament. Yet today, almost a year after the initially revised bill was introduced, we find Bill C-2 still under amendment by a government which knows not where it is going.
In commenting on the bill, I and my colleagues hope to outline where we feel Bill C-2, if passed, would create economic and legal difficulties. Any law, to be meaningful and to be obeyed, must set out in clear language the nature of the offences it is intended to cover. Bill C-2 fails to do that. The bill would give the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission power to set policy with respect to competition in this country without recourse to parliament. The bill's wording is so vague that the commission could virtually write the laws of the land without even the minister knowing what is happening. The proposed legislation overlaps provincial jurisdiction, does not fit into a comprehensive industrial policy for Canada, and may prevent desirable long-term restructuring of the Canadian economy.
Before elaborating on and raising other points with respect to Bill C-2, let us review how we got into this position. In commenting on this legislation I would remind the House that my party, when in power, laid the cornerstone of Canada's present combines legislation when it passed an act prohibiting conspiracies and combinations in restraint of trade. The legislation defined as unlawful any agreement to limit unduly facilities for transporting, producing, storing or selling any article, or to restrain commerce on it, or to unreasonably enhance its price.
Also forbidden was any agreement to unduly prevent or lessen competition in relation to an article or to the price of insurance upon persons or property. Realizing how impatient the minister gets, and indeed how impatient the governments gets, with any comment from opposition members in this parliament-and today he said he would
October 22, 1974

like us to speed up second reading of this bill-I would refer the minister to the earlier words of his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The Prime Minister, in his book "Approaches to Politics," at page 79 wrote:
The point is that in a parliamentary democracy the opposition is the last and most important bulwark against arbitrary tyranny; through it the people reserve the right to criticize from moment to moment the way they are governed-through it they nip legislative and administrative abuses in the bud.
Knowing, as he does, that he has a brutal majority in the House to push this or any legislation through, may I suggest to the minister that he pay particular heed to the comments of opposition members, who may not only save him future embarrassment but, more importantly, may save the people of Canada from the consequences of wrongfully conceived and wrongfully administered legislation. So in this context let us first review the record of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs which was created in December, 1967, by the then Registrar General, the present Minister of Finance.
At that time the Registrar General indicated that the net budget for the new department would be $1 Vi million to $2 million. He spoke glowingly of what the new department could do for the consumers of Canada. I would point out that in the estimates currently before us for the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, we find the budget is over $45 million. The number of employees hired by the department has steadily increased and is now over 2,400.
Between 1967 and today, one might well ask, how has the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, or the government itself, performed on behalf of Canadian consumers? Have they held down prices, for example? The record is that since 1967 the consumer price index in Canada has gone up 45.2 per cent, almost three times the rate of increase in the previous seven years. Food prices have gone up 61.6 per cent since December, 1967, compared with 19.8 between 1961 and 1968. One, clearly, cannot give much credit to the new Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs with respect to price controls. But what about the other activities of this department?
Based on the estimates, we know that $17.5 million in this calendar year is being spent on consumer affairs. If we look at the last annual report published by the department-I am referring to the 1972-73 report for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1973-we find the department had only 13,868 written inquiries from consumers across the country. When one thinks of it, one realizes this is an amazingly small number of complaints compared to the billions of commercial transactions in the nation every year. Think of the cost! It would appear that it costs the taxpayers of Canada $1,250 for each complaint made to the department in written form. Based on the number of personnel in the bureau dealing with consumer affairs, one employee seems to be handling 1 Vi complaints per month.

speechtext:
that Bill C-201, to amend the Bank of Canada Act be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, Bill C-201 is probably the most important bill that has been introduced in the House of Commons for a great many years. When financial matters are involved, it is obvious that everyone agrees that the role of finance is of prime importance for the economic, political and social development throughout this country, and in all spheres of economic activity.
I notice in the Chamber this afternoon two ministers who usually criticize the Social Credit, without considering it, of course. The purpose of this bill is to invite the minister to study it and then the government to implement it. Mr. Speaker, this bill states in section 1, and I quote:
"(i) make loans or advances for periods not exceeding sixty years to the Government of Canada or the government of any province based on the real ccredit of Canada or the province at a rate of interest which does not exceed the cost of administration;"
-to replace the existing section in the Bank of Canada Act... which states at Paragraph 18 (1) (t) the following:
(t) make loans or advances for periods not exceeding six months to the Government of Canada or the government of any province on the

pledge or hypothecation of readily marketable securities issued or guaranteed by Canada or any province;"
Paragraph 18 (1) (j) at present reads as follows, and I quote:
"(j) make loans to the Government of Canada or the government of any province, but such loans outstanding at any one time shall not, in the case of the Government of Canada, exceed one-third of the estimated revenue of such government for its fiscal year, and shall not in the case of any provincial government exceed one-fourth of such government's estimated revenue for its fiscal year; and such loans shall be repaid before the end of the first quarter after the end of the fiscal year of such government;"
Mr. Speaker, under the present Act, a province or Canada could borrow up to one third of its total budget. If the total Canadian budget is $21 billion, the government could borrow directly from the bank of Canada $7 billion, but for no more than six months. Such is the inconsistency of the Bank of Canada Act. Why can the Bank of Canada grant loans for 50 or 60 years to any country in the world and cannot grant it to the government of Canada which legislate over this same Bank of Canada?
Take the province of Quebec, for example. With a budget of $10 billion, it could borrow $2.5 billion a year from the Bank, under the Act, but for no more than six months whereas loans of 50 to 60 years are granted to countries twice smaller than Quebec and with a population two times smaller.
Mr. Speaker, Creditists are often laughed at because they speak about the Bank of Canada. But this is an institution established by the Canadian government, a bank regulated by laws of this Parliament. Every decision of this Parliament concerning the Bank of Canada has to be adhered to. But this government says: As to the Bank of Canada and its monetary policy, we do not have our say because we do not want to. We are free to tell the Bank what it should do to maintain an economically sound Canada, a profitable Canada, and to serve the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, we are presently witnessing the quarrels between provincial and federal governments. What are they quarrelling about? The use of the French language? No. The development of mining resources in Northwestern Canada? No. Western oil? There is some, of course, but they always come to an understanding in the end.
But all Canadian provinces without exception, even the richest ones, are blaming the federal government for not assuming its responsibilities.
Last Thursday evening I was a participant on a Pierre Berton Show originating from Toronto, program scheduled for viewing this week. I was with Mr. Harrandence, a lawyer and former Saskatchewan conservative leader turned separatist in Calgary. He used the same expressions as our own Quebec separatists. His comments did not surprise me. We can hear the same in Quebec.
The Quebec pequistes keep on saying that Ottawa is taking everything away from us to give it to Western Canada. On the other hand, this Canadian from the West was saying exactly the same thing: Ottawa is taking everything away from us to give it to Eastern Canada, to support the province of Quebec. These people do not real-
Bank of Canada Act
ize that there are in Quebec for instance huge quantities of natural resources, as compared with Alberta. There is oil in Alberta. But there is electricity in Quebec, and we send some to Ontario from which we do not buy anything. We have some more to sell and we sell some to the United States, and in view of the James Bay development, Quebec will be selling some to the United States because I feel that, clearly, by the time the James Bay project is completed and at the rate things are going, it will definitely belong to the United States.
Again recently, Mr. Bourassa made a trip to New York City to negociate a $150 million loan at a 10 per cent interest rate for a period of 25 years. Why did he go there? Because the Bank of Canada cannot lend money for more than a 6-month period. That is why we have to go to the United States. Mr. Bourassa might not be there 25 years from now, but the man who will replace him will have paid $265 million in interests only, on a loan of $150 million.
Mr. Speaker, this does not make sense. On what do the Americans base their credit to finance the James Bay Project? On the James Bay project. These are the resources which guarantee the loan. They are not American resources. Mr. Bourassa is not coming back from the United States with wheelbarrows filled with banknotes. He is coming back with a promissory note made to the order of the Americans and endorsed by the Quebec people. We shall have to reimburse $415 million to repay the $150 borrowed. If the federal government would allow Mr. Bourassa to borrow money from the Bank of Canada for 50 or 60 years, in the same manner as that bank is allowed to make loans to India or South American countries, based on the same resources as those considered by American lenders, that is the James Bay's resources, those conflicts would settle down and jealousy between the provinces would no longer exist because they would have the right to become self-determined, to decide for themselves. If only the Bank of Canada was put into the provinces' service. But no, the Bank of Canada follows the Americans even in respect of interest rates.
This afternoon, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) was answering my colleague from Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin) who had asked whether interest rates were not one of the causes of inflation. The Minister of Finance answered: "No, they are rather a consequence". Such an answer from a minister is startling. The first cause of inflation is the interest. When will the James Bay project become worth the $50 or $60 billion spent to complete the installations? When will the $150 million recently borrowed by Mr. Bourassa be worth $415 million? That is the cause of inflation. But the government says it is a consequence.
Municipalities also have troubles with their borrowings. They must even pay 13 or 14 per cent interest rates nowadays. Money does not multiply. I don't know if someone can understand that. Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas stated that too. That is true. If I loan an amount of money to someone and if I am paid a small interest, that is normal because I use something I own.
But banks have an ink-well as well as a pen and they do some figuring. This is exactly what has been done in the United States when Mr. Bourassa was granted a loan of
28305-40'/:
