$150 million last week, namely 16 for 1, at a 10 per cent rate of interest.
Mr. Speaker, no democratic country in the world can survive such a system and it is not taken seriously. If my Creditist friends talk about social credit, about monetary reform, they say: Oh, they are going to talk about the Bank of Canada. But is the Bank of Canada our Canadian institution? And when the Bank of Canada decides to raise the interest rates, who is giving it such an order? Parliament? The Bank of Canada must take its orders from the government, and if the interest rate is so high it is because of the government who allows the Bank of Canada to "flounder". This is its responsibility and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) knows it.
While I am talking about that, he is at his seat. He winks at me in order to tell me that I am right. He does not rise to say: I shall put that advice into practice. If the government fears to do such a thing-though we are only 11-let us be given the chance and we will do it quickly. We shall not take orders from the Americans to decide which interest rate will be charged to the Canadians. Are we not able to have a domestic financial system so that our natural wealth be put at the service of Canadians? Who is preventing this?
The international market is operating well. So let us go on in that way. But in Canada who prevents the Bank of Canada from acting in the best interests of the Canadian people? Who is benefitting from the present credit given to the government? The people? No. It benefits the private banks, at the people's expense. Here is how it is done: It is often claimed that the public debt does not mean a thing; that is what I have been hearing for at least 35 years and there is nothing bad in that, since we owe them to us. We are indebted to ourselves!
It is known that many citizens own Canada savings bonds. Mr. Speaker, is it known that nearly all Canada savings bonds are used mostly as collateral for bank loans? So, who holds the levers, who has the power to create money in Canada? The private banks where the government goes regularly begging on bended knee every 89 or 91 days to borrow money for the same period of time. A psychosis then builds up amongst the people. Then, at some point, things come to a stop for lack of liquidity. What is liquidity? Is that ever explained? Never! People are told: The banks have no more money. They can no longer loan money. There is no money! Then, all of a sudden, there is all kinds of it.
But who decides that? The Americans? The Americans must be called up to find out what their rates of interest are. We are a bunch of sheep, and we have a Parliament of sheep, who follows the Americans. If they take one small step forward, so do we. Then we are told about our Canadian sovereignty! Masters at home! Masters at home when the United States own us about 100 times over!
Mr. Speaker, awhile ago I said that Canadians bought Canada savings bonds. I bought some too. We own ourselves. The pay is poor, but still we own ourselves. The Canadian citizens bought them with their savings, with their hard-earned money, and those same savings are used to create debts, are used mostly as collateral for the banks. The banks can cash the bonds as they see fit, as often as they wish.

A large part of the public debt is payable to the chartered banks. We know that a $1,000 Canada savings bond, for instance, constitutes a reserve for the private banking system, which enables them to multiply by 16 the $1,000 of savings bonds I have. The bank has the right to loan $16,000 on the strength of these savings bonds. I think it is fairly clear. Nobody can dispute this, since it can act this way because of the law.
The major part of the debt is directly payable to chartered banks in the following way: The government floats an issue worth $1 billion or $1 million. The Bank of Canada buys it immediately and deposits this in the account of the government. This immediately creates a reserve for the private banking system which has the right to multiply this by 16, or give $16 million in credit for $1 million in bonds. Then, the government borrows $5 or $6 million in new credits made by the private bank and created by the private banking system. Afterwards, the Bank of Canada will have the responsibility for only $1 million as a guarantee for the new credits of chartered banks.
We admit this. It is stated that the Bank of Canada is the servant of the Canadian banking system. What ever the Bankers Association says, the Bank of Canada jumps to it in short order. I do not recall exactly the name of the Governor of the Bank of Canada who is on all fours before the banking system. Never tell me that the Bank of Canada decides which way the financial or monetary policy of Canada will go because that is wrong. Chartered banks control Canadian finance because they are directly or indirectly, the original source of nearly all the money in our country.
While the ordinary citizen gets his money through his work, the banks create their money by methods that cost almost nothing-the pen and the inkwell and the clerk who uses them. The Bank of Canada says, you must draw numbers, so the government draws numbers. It is only the clerk's salary that has to be paid. Banks produce money with methods that cost almost nothing. They can take advantage of that extraordinary privilege to acquire public funds and become master financiers, and governments at all levels thus offend against justice and reason. Actually, it is highway robbery. We do not want to indenture ourselves and our descendants to the chartered banks. Our governments have their own credit and this credit is much more real than the one offered by chartered banks.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I shall not abuse my colleagues' generosity. I
October 22, 1974

would like, however, to take the time to explain the contents of Bill 201. We shall then hear the opponents of this bill, aimed at making money available for the benefit of man, woman and child, and see what treatment it gets from the government and opposition members. As I mentioned before, we do not wish to be enslaved any more by banks. The question now is who should have control. This Parliament has not been elected to serve banks. We have been elected, each one of us, to serve our constituents, the people of Canada and the country as a whole. To serve this country of ours, to serve it well, we have to relieve it from the paws of rapacious finance people. Such being the aim, let us take the necessary steps. There is no room here for partisanship. Everything centers upon creating a sound economic system, based on something real, that will open the door not to internal strife among Canadians, not to endless strikes, not to killings, but to training Canadians capable of working together for the benefit and well-being of themselves and Canada itself.
Furthermore, as I said earlier, the government of Canada already has in the Bank of Canada an institution that can adequately finance our economic development, without usury or other undesirable conditions.
Mr. Speaker, I am talking about changes advocated by close to 600,000 Social Crediters in the province of Quebec and others, of which 450,000 live in Quebec alone. Those people have been making those proposals for a long time. We are told: You keep repeating the same things over and over again. On the other hand, our critics never change their tune either. They say: "No money!" We reply: Make money! If there is none, create it and use the Bank of Canada!
If the bank is not put to use, the Social Crediters are not responsible; the government is.
The changes put forward in this bill will eliminate the continuous disputes among the various levels of government in Canada as to who should pay the bill of government programs. The fact that money is the perennial concern of governments indicates indeed through their frequent statements, that they are unable to answer all the needs of the people because of lack of money.
Let us have a look at those famous federal-provincial conferences that are held under different excuses and where the delegates always end up quarrelling about money the way hungry dogs fight for an old bone. By eliminating the artificial scarcity of funds available to governments, we would put an end to those shameful scenes.
Moreover, the activities of local governments will depend less on favors granted by more centralizing governments. In other words, the governments will respond more effectively to the aspirations of the citizens in their own territory, our ridings, our provinces and our country.
Mr. Speaker, to implement Bill C-201 means that Canada whose budget will eventually reach $30 billion, could borrow one third each year from the Bank of Canada that is $10 billion at an interest rate not exceeding the administration costs. The pencil pusher's pay would be the federal government's share. The province of Quebec, with a $10 billion budget, could borrow 2.5 billion each year from the Bank of Canada. This amount would cer-
Bank of Canada Act
tainly help the province of Quebec or British Columbia; 25 per cent of the provincial budget would certainly help all the provinces and the Bank of Canada would play its role, serving the interests of Canada and not those of the financiers.
The Bank of Canada could be used to fight inflation efficiently because inflation is built in the monetary system itself. We are suffering its consequences. It is not the interests that are suffering its consequences, it is not the Bank of Canada, it is us! So, if we are suffering its consequences and if we have a responsible government-if it is an irresponsible government that is another matter- but if the government is responsible, it must do something, it must introduce measures aimed at making the Bank of Canada serve Canada, the provinces, the municipalities and the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I always enjoy the speeches made by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), and the speech he made today was no exception. Bill C-201 is without doubt an interesting bill. All its implications certainly could not be dealt with effectively in the space of one hour. The issue he raises, including the control of the banks, the relation between the chartered banks and the Bank of Canada, the extent of United States influence in our economy, and so on, are of great importance and must be the subject of public concern.
The bill itself is very short. Nevertheless, some portions of it immediately attract attention. I note that the Bank of Canada would be permitted to make loans for a period not exceeding 60 years. This is in contrast to section 18 which provides for a period of not longer than six months. Of course, section 18(1)(j) deals with the range within which loans can be made over periods not to exceed three months beyond the fiscal year. The hon. member's idea is an interesting one, but I am not sure it is realistic, at least at this stage.
When we talk about the Bank of Canada we must consider the relative size of the operations of that Bank as opposed to those of the chartered banks and other financial institutions. One set of figures setting out the relative size of the financial intermediaries shows that the Bank of Canada is about 4.6 per cent of all the financial institutions in Canada, whereas the chartered banks make up about 28.9 per cent. Trust and mortgage loan companies and credit unions account for 12.2 per cent, finance companies 4.9 per cent, investment companies 4.3 per cent, life insurance companies 13.6 per cent-an item to be concerned about-private trusteed pension funds 8.9 per cent, for a total of 77 per cent, with other groups at 22 per cent.
These are similar to United States figures. The Federal Reserve Bank occupies the position of holding 5.1 per cent of the intermediary assets. Their chartered banks have about 31 per cent, as opposed to 28.9 per cent in the Canadian system. The Bank of Canada and also the Federal Reserve Bank do not loom substantially in the whole banking scene in this country or in the United States; they rank fifth or sixth among the groups involved in the banking business.

October 22, 1974
Bank of Canada Act
I think we have to look at our banking system to see how efficient it is and how it responds to the needs of governments and private citizens in this country. I, for one, am not a great apologist for the banking system because I think it has many inadequacies, but I am an apologist for the fact that we have to live for today and deal with things as they are.

I am the first person to believe in change. There are many things that I would like to see changed and I could suggest one or two, although I may not have too many solutions.
On the credit side-and I use the word credit not in terms of financial credit-I think we can say that there are certain aspects of the banking system that are good. I think operationally banks are efficient. The cost of operating banks is relatively small in terms of the total business done, and this is one of the plusses of the banking system.
There is a fairly good allocation of efficiency. In other words, our banks provide a fairly decent national capital market. The branch system is well spread throughout the country. It is possible to deposit money and to have almost instant payment of those dollars in any other part of the country. Perhaps this is an advantage we have over the American system, where you have a lot of smaller banks and it is not that easy to exchange money. I think those are two positive aspects.
There is something to be said for concern about regional efficiency in our banking system. In other words, does money invested by investors or deposited in the banks in Canada tend to stay in a region or move to other regions of the country? As someone who lives at the doorstep to the west and who is affected a great deal by western Canada, I can share very much the concern of western Canadians about what happens to their deposits. Do they stay in the west, being circulated in the west, or do they tend to gravitate to that great centre of the world known as Toronto? This is the kind of question we must ask ourselves.
Having done a little research on this subject I was rather surprised at the fact that in western Canada-I have not done the same kind of research into the situation in eastern Canada-there seems to be a reasonable circulation of deposits made in that part of the country. For instance, in the province of Manitoba, which has about 4.5 per cent of the population of this country, according to statistics as at December 31, 1972, 4.8 per cent of the loans made by chartered banks were made in that province. In British Columbia we have 14.1 per cent of the population, and 13.4 per cent of loans were made in that province. About 26.5 per cent of the total population of Canada lives in the west, and 30.2 per cent of money loaned in Canada is loaned in that area. At the same time 29 per cent of the branches of Canadian banks are located in western Canada, even though the population is, as I said, about 26 per cent of all Canada.

I do not think you can isolate the chartered banks from the Bank of Canada, nor does the hon. member for Temis-camingue. He constantly associated the two. I am trying to deal with the whole banking system, and this is a necessary part of any such discussion.

I am very much concerned with the fact that chartered banks in Canada, under the aegis of the Bank of Canada, seem to be involved in financing foreign takeovers of Canadian companies. At times it would seem easier to get a loan if you happen to represent a foreign company in this country than if you represent a Canadian company, given the same credit rating. This is one of our great concerns.
We have all seen examples of financing not being available to a Canadian company which was forced to sell out to a foreign company or corporation that in turn could immediately go to the same bank and successfully negotiate the financing of a similar project. This is the kind of thing that should be of concern to all Canadians.
We must also be concerned about the activity of foreign banks in Canada, to the extent that we are, in theory, trying to have a Canadian banking system that is all Canadian. What we have in fact is a whole system of near-banks moving into Canada, in one form or another, and in an obtuse sort of way taking over a great deal of the financing operations of the country. As Canadians we should be very concerned about this.
Let me conclude by referring to my last concern, and this is a concern I think which bothers most of us, including the hon. member for Temiscamingue. I have in mind the tremendous amount of capital, something like $100 billion, required to finance energy operations in Canada in the next 10 years. The Bank of Canada and chartered banks in Canada will have to play a much bigger role in this operation than they are playing at the present time. If we are to see projects undertaken similar to the James Bay development project in the future-and in that case we are talking about $12 billion, if we are to see projects undertaken such as an oil pipeline-here we are talking about $10 billion or $12 billion, and if we are to have the development of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, and in that case we would be talking about $6 billion or $8 billion, these things will have a tremendously distorting effect on our whole economy.

speechtext:
I have not had the opportunity to congratulate you, Madam Speaker, and I should like to do so now. It is nice to see someone of your wisdom and charm presiding over our meetings. Let me say that you grace the chair.
I am sure that the Leader of the Social Credit Party in putting forward Bill C-201 is making a serious attempt to do something for Canada by doing something about inflation. I have no doubt that the honourable member is a man of experience who knows something about money, knows what is good money and what is bad, and is not at all stupid. I understand he knows a good deal about investment.
In regard to this bill I do not think anyone can really estimate the true extent of the real credit of Canada. Let me suggest it is even more difficult to calculate our real credit worth than it is to say how much oil there may be in the ground either in Alberta, the Arctic or the Mackenzie Delta. We know the real estate value of Canada. We know what is in the banks and we can estimate fairly accurately the value of our current crops including our fisheries, agriculture, forestry and mining, but it is by no means an easy thing to calculate the real credit of Canada.
I feel that a philosophy of this political shade was not really tried, whether it be in Alberta or British Columbia, because those areas enjoyed a climate of prosperity, and the socreds ran things in an orthodox manner fiscally. I believe it is the intention of the sponsor of this bill to put forward a completely experimental idea. I am in favour of animal experimentation. I believe in the use of biological animals, to the extent that rabbits, dogs and white mice should be used for experimentation in an attempt to find some physiological way to assist medical science. On the other hand I do not believe that the people of Canada should be the guinea pigs for any experiment such as that embodied in this bill. I suggest it is purely experimental, and I see no reason why this should be foisted upon us by any group.
While I believe that the entire experience and wisdom of mankind are necessary to solve our present world troubles, particularly those associated with the world's inflationary cycle we are now experiencing anyone who would try to separate Canada from other countries in the world would not be doing Canada a kindness, even though he might have a very serious and patriotic concern or motivation.
I believe this bill is designed to fight inflation. If we regard it as such an attempt then we must return to the question: can we separate our Canadian inflation from world inflation? This bill is only for Canada. I think this bill would put us right down the drain if we were to adopt it. Let us see first of all whether we have any connection

October 22, 1974
Bank of Canada Act
with the rest of the world so far as our inflation is concerned. It is very important for us to decide whether we agree or disagree upon this.
We know very well that inflation is beyond the complete reversal we would all like to see. I think it has been well demonstrated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), and by everything that has gone on in the last few years, that our fight against inflation really must be carried on in a very measured and methodical manner and not by the adoption of some experimental method of changing our banking system or our way of borrowing money.
In other words, we are completely interdependent, as has been mentioned by the Minister of Finance, with other countries of the world. We cannot separate our economies. We cannot afford to adopt some very different method of taxation, wage and price controls, or of banking which would place us apart from the rest of the world.
We need the other countries and they need us. I think this is the first thing we must admit. We cannot employ ways to fight inflation in Canada that would erode our prosperity. We are still prosperous. I do not think anyone would deny that.
I have had conversations with a member of the delegation which recently returned from Japan, and I had an opportunity to spend three days in Tokyo last January. I realize that Japan is going through a fairly difficult economic situation. However, it has more or less accepted this situation with open arms. The attitude of the people there is that certainly prices are up, but so are wages and profits. They realize this is a world-wide condition. They are not using any new-fangled ideas to fight the situation.
The Japanese are being careful in respect of their governmental expenses, just as we are here. They are attempting to live as closely as possible to their budget but they are not attempting to slow down inflation by increasing unemployment, and are not attempting to slow down the prosperity cycle.
I think it would be rather ridiculous for us in Canada to change our ideas when we have successfully, over the past three years, fought off inflation to the extent that we are doing better than almost any other country in the world. Here and there in respect of certain commodities some countries are doing better, but this relates to two or three commodities at the most. I am talking mainly about the United States of America.
We are in an extremely fortunate position with relation to inflation. This is because of the common sense attitude of the government. I think we would have been in a very sorry state had we brought in wage and price controls. I believe almost everyone on the opposite side of the House would admit that now. They are probably glad that this was not done. There has been a great deal of talk about it as a means of fighting inflation, but I think the common sense attitude of the Minister of Finance is the better approach; that is, to get people to realize that slowing down the economy would simply cause people to suffer and bring on more unemployment.

We must increase our productivity not only in respect of farm, forest and mineral products but also in other fields. If we do these things and tighten our belts a little we can weather the storm. I think there are signs of that storm abating now. Although we have now, and will have for some months, increases in prices of certain commodities, I think we can all admit there will be a sort of flattening out onto a plateau instead of a steep rise over the next few months. It would seem to me that the common sense attitude of the world is bearing fruit.
I am glad to see the Minister of Finance selected as chairman of the interim committee of the International Monetary Fund. I think that his common sense will be valuable and will enhance Canada's reputation, especially when it is remembered that here is a country with resources of all kinds which we cannot even compute, a country of small population, a country which does not push anyone around, and a country which wants to contribute as well as it can to the underdeveloped countries.
I believe it is very important that we make use of some of the financial opportunities we have. One opportunity I really wish to turn thumbs down on is the experiment in our monetary system that was talked about by the hon. member opposite. It would seem to me to be important to realize that Canada needs investment more than ever.
Canada does not have a great amount of money. Much of our private capital is invested in the United States of America. We should realize there are people clamouring for an opportunity to invest in our country. We might start with the U.K., France, Germany and Japan. Then there are the Arab oil countries which have had such great success in bringing money into their coffers. This money must be re-invested and recycled. I believe Canada is one of the best places for the Arabs to invest their money. Madam Speaker, I see it is six o'clock. I am sorry I have taken so long.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before our break at five o'clock I was saying that the
October 22, 1974

government had introduced legislation with the concept of which few in this House would disagree. However, I feel that we in the opposition must assess the legislation to see whether it will in fact perform a useful function in increasing competition in the country. I gave certain background material, and I commented on the fact that while the government is proposing increased regulations with respect to such things as misleading advertising and misrepresentation, it does not seem to include its own activities for review in the same context.
I gave certain examples of federal government forms of advertising that I felt could be challenged and, in fact, may be challenged. Another would be the Canada Savings Bonds advertisements which refer to security, income and flexibility. In the current ads they say that for tax purposes the government of Canada proposes to permit taxpayers to treat cash bonus payments either as interest income or capital gains. They then go on to say that there will be certain exemptions from taxation.
I would point out to the House that they are referring to a possible budgetary measure that may be included in the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) some time between now and the middle of November. But is it fair to include that comment in an advertisement at present, knowing that the government could even be brought down before November 15? Surely members of the government learned a lesson when they were defeated on the last budget on May 9. Yet we find they have no compunction about including, in an ad for general readership in Canada, a suggestion that something is a fact when it is clearly only a possibility.
I should like to make a quick review of some of the steps that have led up to the bill before us today. In his opening remarks the minister referred to the interim report on competition policy put out by the Economic Council of Canada in July, 1969. I would point out to hon. members that it is very clear in chapter 1 of that report that it is in fact an interim report. It states:
It is designated an interim document to indicate: (a) that further reports are to be issued, and (b) that these reports are likely to include further discussions of combines, mergers, monopolies and restraint of trade. The Council's next report will discuss patents, copyrights, trademarks and registered industrial designs. A fourth and final report will then be issued containing further observations and recommendations, notably on the subject of consumer affairs, and a general summing-up of the interrelations between the three main elements of Reference and their place in the broader spectrum of the government economic policies.
I feel that we might ask: have in fact further reports been issued by the Economic Council of Canada and, if not, why not? That question was put to Dr. Raynauld, present chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, earlier this month. I asked the following question in the Finance Committee:
Have you prepared a further report on competition policy, which was prepared back in July, 1969? ... what is your attitude to Bill C-2, which is the current version of the government's competition legislation, which, as you know, came out of the original study?
Dr. Raynauld: This is a good question. The problem is that I will have to decline because I think I am correct in saying that there has been no further report.
Combines Investigation Act
He then went on to say:
On competition itself there have been no further reports ... Since my appointment as Chairman of the Economic Council there has never been any mention that we would do further work in this particular field and, therefore, I have no view about the present bill which is before the House.
I mention that because surely it is odd that a minister and a government would refer to this report as often as they do, using it as a basis for the legislation that we have before us today, and yet the report on its face was an interim report, and when we ask the chairman of the Economic Council of Canada whether he has continued with further reports, he is almost startled by the question and admits that nobody even asked for further reports after the interim one was in hand.
As I mentioned earlier, the original bill that was introduced with respect to competition contained a stage I and a stage II. Stage II dealt with monopolies and combines. We are told that that legislation will be forthcoming. But it becomes a little confusing because the government tends to change ministers rather rapidly.
The hon. member who until recently was minister of consumer and corporate affairs, told us that stage II of the competition legislation would be in place by the end of this year. According to an interview carried in the Globe and Mail today, the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has said that in no way will this be done. He is still talking and intends to talk to more businessmen. That shows the government's quandary in seeking the proper approach to competition in this country. The government itself does not know what to do. That is why this bill is premature; the government has no over-all perspective of what should be done with regard to competition policy.
As I said earlier, stage II of the legislation is in the wings. Presumably this bill, also, is subject to amendment by the minister at the committee stage. The minister ought to table those amendments forthwith. This afternoon he said he was willing to compromise. I have no idea what he means by that. If he wishes, let him make those compromises. Let us see how Bill C-2 will look, as he hopes, in its final form. Then the House can deal with it as it sees fit.
Last time a bill similar to this was given second reading and sent to committee, we found that some of its provisions which were to amend the Combines Investigation Act were subsequently to be amended by the antiprofiteering bill introduced in the last parliament, read the second time and sent to committee.

Combines Investigation Act
Let me refer again to the interim report of the Economic Council of Canada. On page 108 the council recommended: -that before preparing new legislation embodying major changes in competition policy, the federal government should take the initiative in proposing that discussions of competition policy and related policies be arranged between the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and appropriate provincial ministers.
We are entitled to an explanation. Why does the government feel justified in acting on the basis of the interim report but, at the same time, ignoring the strong recommendations in that report calling on the government to consult with the provinces before legislating? Not only has the government failed to consult with the provinces; it has failed to consult effectively with business, industry, unions, farmers, and consumers. It ought to have consulted these groups before bringing forward this legislation.
I now wish to touch on the federal-provincial relations aspect of this bill and the constitutionality of some of its provisions. Proposed Part IV. 1 raises difficult constitutional questions. In its report the Economic Council felt sufficiently uncertain about the creation of an administrative type of tribunal that it recommended a constitutional reference to resolve the doubt. If the legislation should be passed, it would be necessary to decide if proposed Part IV. 1 is proper under the federal government's existing criminal law powers, under its trade and commerce powers, or under the peace, order and good government provisions of the British North America Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext: It is proper under all three.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Proposed Part IV. 1 does not appear to be concerned with criminal offences, in the sense that term has been traditionally described in our jurisprudence. There are many cases at the privy council level and at the supreme court level dealing with court interpretations of the federal government's trade and commerce power. These decisions do not provide much of a precedent for what is covered by proposed Part IV. 1. Generally, they confirm the federal government's power to regulate the importation and interprovincial movement of commodities and, in turn, the provinces' lack of power to do so.
Proposed Part IV. 1 is not confined to interprovincial agreements or marketing practices, and a long line of marketing cases sets the precedent that federal regulation under the trade and commerce power cannot be rationalized on the grounds that the subject matter has an interprovincial character.
That leaves us with the peace, order and good government power. This would be the court's last resort in trying to justify proposed Part IV. 1 as being within federal competence. Therefore, as the powers to be given to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission form such an important part of this proposed legislation, it appears that much of the bill rests on a shaky constitutional basis.
Is that the way for the government to lay a foundation for competition policy in Canada? Would it not have been better to have had prior provincial consultation with a view to constitutional change, if necessary, in order to ensure a sound approach to those matters proposed under Part IV.l?
The extension of the Combines Investigation Act, as proposed in Bill C-2, into the service field would aggravate

the problem which now exists with respect to the overlapping of federal and provincial regulatory laws. If the federal government wants to avoid embarrassments brought on by passage of this bill, it should make it clear that the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act which cover services will not apply if they conflict with provincial law.
British Columbia recently enacted a Trade Practices Act, and in Ontario there is Bill 55, the Ontario Business Practices Act. These acts cover fields similar to those covered by the provisions of proposed sections 36 and 37 in Bill C-2. It is unfortunate that the federal authorities did not co-ordinate their legislative program in this area with that coming under provincial jurisdiction. We do not need two sets of criminal sanctions to govern essentially the same type of behaviour.
Proposed sections 29.1 and 31.1 contain new enforcement and remedial provisions which have attracted considerable hostility, as the minister is no doubt aware. The first section mentioned would give an interim injuctive power, while the second would entitle an aggrieved party to recover damages arising out of the commission of a Part V offence with regard to a breach of a Restrictive Trade Practices Commission order. In both cases we have evidence of the unsatisfactory result obtained by trying to force a civil remedy into the tight confines of the criminal law.
A further constitutional problem arises with respect to the conferring of original trial criminal jurisdiction on the federal court which, until now, has been presumed to be a prerogative which belongs exclusively to the provinces. The main issue arises because of the conflicting provisions of the BNA Act, which may only be resolved through constitutional change.
This all shows that in bringing forward this bill the minister is taking us into uncharted waters. He mentioned earlier that the previous minister of consumer and corporate affairs had outlined certain features of this legislation at second reading but he did not elaborate on the details.
I do not intend to go into detail on what we said on second reading, but I think it is important that we reiterate some of the points made so effectively by the member who represented the riding of St. Paul's at that time. On March 13, 1974, he said as reported at page 484 of Hansard, that the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission would be creating:
-to all intents and purposes, a new, highly centralized agency which has the potentiality of interposing itself into a major segment of Canadian political and economic life... the bill will permit the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission to alter or restructure market distribution systems in Canada in an unprecedented fashion.
We reiterate that point, Mr. Speaker. As reported at the same page he pointed out that decisions are delegated to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission under the bill. He stated that in his view the government would wrongfully be abdicating its own responsibilities to make policy decisions of this magnitude, and he asked that it reconsider vesting decision making of this sort in the commission and consider vesting it in the Governor in Council. We reiterate that request, Mr. Speaker.
October 22, 1974

At page 485 he pointed out that:
-the commission is left to make its own rules for the regulation of its proceedings and the performance of its duties and functions under the act.
Again we reiterate that. He also stated.
There are various classes of service industries which are exempted for one reason or another.
The largest and most important classes, the ones I have just referred to, that are controlled by provincial legislation at the present time, are unfortunately not exempted. This will cause confusion.
At page 486 he stated:
We think it is high time in Canada that the government applied anti-combines laws to the labour unions.
We would be most interested to hear from the minister precisely why he has persisted in exempting the labour unions from this type of competition legislation. Later he said, as reported on the same page:
-we believe the minister should at least provide an acceptable rationalization as to why the banks should continue to be treated differently, under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance. This is a different and softer type of combines regime than exists for other financial institutions such as the trust companies and insurance companies.
I felt we should get this on the record once again, Mr. Speaker. Let me emphasize that the points raised in more detail by the hon. member at that time are reiterated today when considering this bill, as far as we are concerned. I would go further and say that we are concerned that the ambiguities contained in Bill C-2 may discourage aggressive business behaviour and create a climate of uncertainty which makes business planning difficult. It will place an unnecessary and undesirable economic burden on the community. Businessmen are naturally reluctant to make commitments when the laws which regulate their behaviour are not clear. The result is that desirable economic activities will likely be curtailed unless the rather ambiguous sections of the bill are clarified.
During the course of debate a number of specific suggestions will be offered by my colleagues. Let me state very briefly that we believe there should be clarification of such terms as "product", "business" of lending money, "unreasonably low", "widespread", "major supplier", "inadequate", "chances" of winning a prize in a promotional contest, and the distinction drawn between local and national advertisers. I am quoting directly from the bill, Mr. Speaker, and suggesting that these terms should be clearly defined.
There is the word "article" for instance. In its present context the word would cover shopping centres, making it a criminal offence to operate a shopping centre in this country. Is that the understanding and wish of the government? According to clauses 32(1) (c) and (d) and 38(6) it would appear to be an offence even to ask people to rent space in a shopping centre so long as the word "article" is not defined to make it clear that that type of operation is not included.
In another of his interviews with the press the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs stated he believes this legislation will not receive as much opposition as previous legislation because "businessmen are tired out". What a strange statement for a minister of the Crown to make!

speechtext:
Having pointed out some of the consequences if this legislation is passed, I should point out that it is particularly the small businessmen who will be hurt by the competition policy proposed by the government. They have been particularly hard hit already by the government's policies.
Although 60 per cent of the work force is employed in small business, we find that between 1962 and 1973 their employers' share of the national income fell from 10.7 per cent to 7.5 per cent. The fact is that this legislation would have extremely harmful effects on the business community, especially the small businessmen.
I mentioned earlier that the bill does not fit in with any overall industrial strategy. In fact, as we know, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) is unique; he takes great credit for having said that the government has no industrial strategy. I mention this because I believe the trade deficit with respect to manufactured articles sold for export is becoming alarming. In 1972 that deficit amount-

October 22, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
ed to 1.5 billion. In 1973 it was $2.2 billion, and in the first half of this year alone it had risen to $2 billion. The only way this country is able to maintain a trade surplus is by selling off a like amount of natural resources.
If the minister is serious in saying this is a bill by which he hopes to catch big business in this country, he should be as good as his word and place a provision in the bill assuring it will not affect small businessmen with assets below a certain amount. Such a provision was included in the Foreign Investment Review Act passed by the last parliament, and I would recommend that a similar course be taken by the minister in any competition legislation he might bring forward.
I mentioned there was an absence of consultation with various sectors of our economy. I would suggest the government consider establishing a national industry and productivity council on a fully functional basis, with a working staff drawn from its own constituent components from government, both federal and provincial, business, industry and labour, and that its purpose be the co-ordination of an effective national industrial policy; that it formulate guidelines for the establishment, location and financing of new industry or the expansion of existing industry; that it provide for the elimination of uncoordinated and counterproductive development in the various regions of Canada; that it work toward the elimination of the atmosphere of confrontation which now exists between government, federal or provincial, management and labour; that it provide for the better equipping of Canadian industry to meet changing economic conditions and for the improvement of the rate of growth in productivity in both the private and the public areas.
This would be a worthwhile step for the government to take, and certainly would be more constructive than bringing in a piece of legislation which might be more harmful than helpful. Judging from the record of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs I suggest it might be preferable if the corporate affairs part were switched to the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice. This would ensure the services of a full-time minister of consumer affairs who would be able to devote all his energy to protecting the interests of the consumer.
There are others in my party who wish to speak. I have attempted to outline our thinking on this legislation. I am sure members who support the government are more than willing to give us ample opportunity to express further views concerning the legislation. After all, five bills have been passed in the last few days; surely they will not mind a few speeches concerning the bill now before us.
In conclusion, let me say that I think competition is a good thing. We in this House, and certainly the members of the party to which I belong, endorse competition.

Mr. Speaker, the first thing that strikes me about the bill we are considering this evening is its title which reads: "An Act to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Bank Act and to repeal an Act to amend an Act to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code." It is also known, euphemistically, as the competition bill.
I should like to examine several questions, one of which asks what competition this bill purports to regulate? Is it competition between competitor and competitor? I suggest that the bill before us serves, in fact, to institutionalize the present situation of competition between buyer and seller, competitor and consumer. Here, Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of the Hansard, reporters, each and every time I use the word "competitor" it should be placed in quotation marks.
Lest hon. members think I displayed a partisan bias in my initial remarks I would ask them to heed the comments made in a speech delivered by an advertising executive to a meeting of the Canadian Grocery Distributors Institute in Toronto in February, 1973. He said, and I quote:
So what's so bad about industry co-operation? After all, your competitors aren't your enemies but your consumers are.
I suggest this was no accidental remark but rather an accurate indication of the mentality of most "competitors" in this "free enterprise" system. Another note to the Hansard reporters: each and every time I utter the words "free enterprise" in this speech, they too should be enclosed in quotation marks.
I am sure the government is well aware of the fact of which the advertising executive spoke. Having read this bill and all the related material, and having heard so much about the great "free enterprise" system, I am led to observe that it is indeed strange that corporations have to be legislated into making some token display of competition with each other. One would expect that by the very definition of "free enterprise" they would be just dying to compete. But that is not so. These so-called "competitors" have to be forced to compete with each other.
When this bill is not attempting to force "competitors" to compete, it is attempting to regulate the aggressive competition which actually exists; that is, the competition of the companies against the consumer. Unfortunately, the only people left in the dark as to the true situation are the Canadian consumers, who daily frequent the marketplace. This, to me, is one of the most reprehensible aspects of this bill-it only pretends to regulate, it does not actually regulate-and the consequent effect is to lull the Canadian consumer into a false sense of security.
In case this House thinks I am dabbling in rhetoric-

I am glad hon. members are applauding because I should like to deal with some of the specific measures which the government holds up to the public with the claim that they are beneficial. We have, for example, the practice of double ticketing. The bill will make it unlawful for a company to sell at other than the lower price of the double ticket. Yet the bill will not
October 22, 1974

prohibit what the Food Prices Review Board, in its report of November 1973, described as the "accepted business practice of revaluing inventories as prices change".
Clearly, the thrust of this legislation should not merely be one of warning the companies that they have to clean up their up front operations, not, of course, unless the government agrees that it is the consumer who is competing with the companies, in which case maintaining the companies' freedom to overprice inventories under the counter rather than over the counter is most consistent.
Let us look at another provision of the bill which, for the life of me, I cannot believe is actually seriously proposed by the government. That is the amendment which would provide the right of action to individuals who suffer as a result of conspiracy on the part of companies. Well, I would suggest to the government that all individuals suffer as a result of conspiracy on the part of companies, and that what is needed is a provision for class actions, not individual actions.
Let us take the example of our three major sugar importers, Atlantic, Redpath and St. Lawrence, who were convicted of price fixing back in 1963. All three companies were fined and placed under a restraining order to prevent future collusion. Yet these three companies are back in court again.
It is my understanding that the prosecutor has estimated the cost to the Canadian consumer of the price fixing activities of the companies at somewhere in the neighbourhood of $125 million between 1960 and 1973. I would suggest-and I am not commenting on the present trial one way or the other-that if this is so and the companies are again convicted, and some rough determination of the bilking yield is made, then it ought to be possible for consumers as a class to demand that their moneys be returned to them, and the fines levied should equal the amount bilked from the public by the price fixers.
I wonder about the sincerity of the government's intentions when it pretends to expect an individual to go about the business of attempting to figure out the dollars he may have lost to the sugar companies over 13 years and then attempt to sue on an individual basis.
Let us take this issue to its logical conclusion. If the government seriously believed that in cases of conspiracy the individual consumer would pursue his right to take the companies to court, what would they propose to do with the resulting glut of court cases? Can we picture, for instance, every individual household head first figuring out what he is owed, and then all proceeding to court at the same time? It boggles the mind somewhat. Obviously it does not boggle the corporate mind; they do not have to worry.
If I view the lack of competition between companies as alarming, there is something I find even more alarming, and that is the government's failure to deal with vertical integration of huge companies. Let me give yet another illustration of the manner in which "competitors" engage in competition, not with other "competitors" but with the consumer. The outstanding example is the George Weston Limited company which, in its annual report, calls 1973 "a gratifying year". And well it might be gratified with after
Combines Investigation Act
tax profits standing at $34.6 million, an increase of 86 per cent over 1972.
The consumer might be deceived into thinking that the Weston company is in a deathlock competition with other manufacturers of food goods. But in fact George Weston Limited is in competition mainly with George Weston Limited.
A quick survey of some of its "competitors" reveals nothing more than a long list of its own subsidiaries, which include some of the biggest, best known and most powerful food manufacturing companies in Canada. There are, for example, Weston Bakeries Limited, the largest bakery in Canada; Weston Foods; McCormicks; William Nielson Limited; British Columbia Packers, Canada's largest fish processor; Connor Brothers Fisheries; Somerville Industries Limited; Westfair Foods; Kelly, Douglas and Company; and of course the Loblaw group. Then there is National Grocers, Atlantic Wholesalers, B.C. Packers with subsidiaries of its own, including Nelson Brothers and Rupert's Certi-Fresh Foods. We then have Connor Brothers, with its subsidiaries W. H. Welch Limited and Lewis, Conners and Sons Limited, plus a host of other associated companies.
What does this mean when the consumer walks into a grocery store, Mr. Speaker?

Yes, the price is right for George Weston. Let me use salmon as an example. The consumer is confronted by an overwhelming array of brand names, a few of which are the following: Carnation, Universal, Surf, Ferndale, Overwaitea, Rose Marie, Red Rose, Pine Tree, High Seas, Sea Lord, Silverline, Fraser Gold, Swallow, Clipper, Tip Top, Streamline, Sea Trader, Queen Charlotte, A & P, Clover Leaf, Maple Leaf, Paramount, Laguna, Sea-Gift, Robin Red, Loblaws and Thunderbird.
But, Mr. Speaker, the confusion does not end there. There is cohoe and keta, sockeye and whitespring. Then there is red salmon or pink salmon, minced or creamed salmon. Then you have a choice of trying to figure out the per ounce price of, would you believe, cans that contain either 15 ounces or 15'/2 ounces, three and three quarter ounces or seven and three quarter ounces. Why three quarters of an ounce, Mr. Speaker? But let me not digress into another area that is badly in need of this kind of government legislation.
Little does the consumer know, as he or she struggles to determine the per ounce price of the different brands and can sizes, that it does not really matter what brand is purchased-the money is going into the same pocket, in this instance the George Weston superpocket. What does this piece of legislation do to encourage competition? Can this government show me one element of the competition bill which encourages competition in the salmon industry?
Further, the Economic Council of Canada, in its report on competition policy of July, 1969, concluded that in many areas of activity "monopolistic tendencies have all but eliminated competitive market responses." For a long time the food industry was not as intensely monopolized as it is today. Today we find farmers being driven off the land as agribusiness takes over. Farmers' markets used to

flourish, as well as door to door food selling, but they have been rapidly replaced by supermarket selling. At one time there were numbers of local cheese factories across this country; now there is only Kraft.
I realize that the minister has promised a review of this legislation with particular reference to an examination of the more fundamental questions which arise in a study of the structural characteristics of our economy. However, I suspect that Bill C-2 is an indicator of what will come in the second stage of the legislation.
I note from this morning's Globe and Mail that the minister intends to initiate extensive discussion with business, of course, before the introduction of the second stage of the legislation can be expected. The minister said, and I quote:
I don't want to bulldoze the second phase because it comes to the crunch of business philosophy. It is an entirely new approach.

The best is yet to come. He is reported as having said:
I consider it as an instrument that the government ought to have, and no more. We need it, for example, for the Food Prices Review Board. If Mrs. Plumptre were to make recommendations pointing out clearly instances of abuse, the government does not have any instrument or any leverage to act. I think we need it as a sort of show-case. Can I use the word window-dressing? We should have this bill for that reason. I really do not want to use it, or look forward to using it, because I have no objection to profits.
It is fairly obvious that when the government removed one minister, putting him in the backbenches, and brought forward this minister it was very much like digging a hole to fill a hole. I think this minister communicates more with the people; his kind of people-the corporate people.
I realize that we are talking here about the competition bill and not the anti-profiteering bill but I suggest that the minister's comments bespeak the mentality of the government in any legislation it undertakes which might protect the consumer from the "competitors."
Let me again refer to the minister's comments in the Globe and Mail. I note he feels that the trend of low fines for combines offences in the past is not a problem of law but, according to him, "a problem of our attitude". He goes on to elaborate that Canadians are not yet accustomed to seeing large fines or jail sentences for these kinds of offences. What a masterful piece of double talk that is!
If Canadians are not accustomed to seeing large fines or jail terms handed out for offences causing suffering to the consumer I suggest it is the fault of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
This leads me to another area of doubt about this bill. The basic legislation has been around for a long time, but I note that the Restrictive Trades Practices Commission has not been noted for its in-department vigour. For instance,

by law that commission is to have three members, but the number has gradually dwindled to one. I note as well that in 1970-1971 the commission spent only 41 per cent of its budget; in 1971-72 it spent only 61 per cent, and again in 1972-73 only 61 per cent of its budget was spent.
It is amazing that one of the few commissions holding a clear responsibility to protect the consumer and save the consumer dollars, engages in saving taxpayer dollars put aside for that purpose. Well might the minister lament the lack of exemplary fines and jail sentences for offenders. His department and the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission are obviously at fault in showing a lack of example in initiative to the rest of the country.
To sum up, this bill with all its complexities does not propose any measure that a self-respecting corporation could not circumvent. Any corporation in this country worth its salt could circumvent any one of the provisions of this bill.
As far as my party is concerned, there ought to be two principles involved when a sincere government sets about to bring forward competition legislation. Firstly, monopolistic control over production, distribution and marketing of goods and services should never be permitted and, secondly, the government must intervene in the marketplace to provide consumers with goods of quality at reasonable prices. This bill does not even remotely approach these principles.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill I should like to congratulate the minister on his appointment and for his fine speech this afternoon. The minister once again has demonstrated his competence and his knowledge, and in the very early opportunity he has had he once again has demonstrated his approach and intellect in meeting the complexities of this legislation.
Tonight we heard a lengthy address by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) regarding this bill. He spent very little time dealing with the bill itself, but carried us forward to a variety of topics, including a general discussion about the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The hon. member referred by some striking financial sleight of hand to the number of complaints received by the department, and then went on to divide the number of complaints into the amount of money spent on the entire consumer services of the department, some $17.5 million, telling the House that this was the total cost of all complaints received in any one year since the department was formed. The hon. member obviously drew this figure from the 1974-75 estimates covering a variety of activities, of which approximately $1 million represents expenditures by the branch which looks after consumer education, information and complaints.
I noticed that the hon. member was not content with referring the House to these striking observations, but also told the citizens of Toronto at a meeting of a chapter of the Institute of Chartered Accountants the same story. I assume that when one reflects on that point raised in that part of the hon. member's speech one can judge the merit of the rest of it.
Again the hon. member referred to a number of problems he foresaw during this parliament, including that in

respect of "a brutal majority," to use his colourful words. I suggest this is a strong phrase to use to describe what is only a moderate majority, but one which I think the Canadian people are gratified to see on this side of the House.
The hon. member referred to the fact that in this competition bill, again to use his colourful words, "we are sailing through uncharted waters". We have heard the minister's comments and we are aware of the endless references in this House to this whole area of competition policy since 1966 when it was introduced by the economic council in its report, reiterated in various pieces of legislation, and again only in the last session in the legislation which received second reading and went to the committee.
Once again this bill has been introduced. Once again the public is to be given the opportunity, both consumers and business organizations, to bring their points of view before the committee. Surely that could hardly be described as uncharted waters.
There were some points of substance raised by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, but they were in what might be termed a derivative fashion since he drew a melancholy note in respect of the words of the former hon. member for St. Paul's who is no longer with us. Unfortunately the people of St. Paul's did not choose to return that particular member, but his words will be immortalized in the Hansard of the thirtieth parliament thanks to the contribution of the hon. member for York-Simcoe.
The minister, in his comments on this bill, did not choose to reiterate in complete detail each and every policy that is contained in the bill because this is all familiar to members of the House. It is hoped when the committee deals with it, and deals with it hopefully expeditiously, this long planned competition policy for Canada will be made into law.
I think there are a great many Canadians who have seen defects in the previous legislation, in the draft bill which was introduced. I happen to be one of those who found a considerable number of defects in the original draft legislation which was brought into this House, but the bill we have before us this evening is one which, on almost every count, is bringing Canadians a first-class competition policy.
Instead of bulldozing a policy through the House the previous minister and the minister before that introduced a draft bill, and allowed the most elaborate possible type of consultation. Out of that elaborate consultation was derived a bill which can now come before parliament without fear that it will be a disservice to the Canadian people.
During the previous committee stage certain proposed amendments were introduced. Some were of a minor or technical nature. Some dealt with specific wording such as the hon. member for York Simcoe asked be considered. I hope these amendments will reappear. I hope that perhaps some others might reappear as well. Most of them are of a minor or technical nature dealing with anomalies in particular spheres of industry which were not contemplated at the time the bill was drafted.

I find it curious that the hon. member for York Simcoe does not want amendments introduced, wants all the amendments introduced today, does not want the bill to receive any positive treatment at the committee stage, and does not want any reaction to contributions made by industrial, business or consumer groups.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) made a speech containing some extremely fishy references and long lists of products. However, I did find one clause of the bill on which he reflected where I too share his dissatisfaction, although I do not think for quite the same extreme reason. I do not find the clause in respect of double ticketing a particularly effective one to be introduced into such an important blueprint for the competition policy of this country.
I hasten to say that I do not support the practice that is known as double ticketing by retail food stores. I think those stores have given their undertaking in this regard, and are not practicing this unfair form of behaviour. In any event I do not think this is a particularly appropriate clause to introduce in a bill of this scale. As the hon. member pointed out, it really does not deal with the question of the revaluing of inventories. I think very few members of this House would suggest that at no time should there be no ability on the part of businesses or industry to revalue their inventories.
Apart from that, I do not think this particular clause deals with the revaluing of inventories but rather deals with a particular practice of a grocery company finding additional stickers on a package and then not choosing to award the customer the lowest of the particular prices. My objection first is that I do not think it is broad enough or important enough to place in a bill of this dimension. Second, I think this often is brought about inadvertently by companies handling hundreds of thousands of items. It might be that every day by accident they are committing this particular offence. To that, extent, and that extent only, would I support some of the comments made by the hon. member for Nickel Belt. I wish to say, however, I believe the Canadian people are aware now that parliament intends to introduce a piece of competition policy that will suit this country and be more akin to the type of advanced concepts in other nations. I suggest that time has arrived. I also suggest I do not believe it will require "a brutal majority", the description used by my hon. friend. I think this bill, its concept, and the amendments which may be made in committee and reintroduced in this House will commend themselves, and I trust will soon be made into law for the benefit of Canada.
