speechtext:
Mr. Speaker what the bill before us attempts to achieve is basically reform in two areas. The first is that area generally referred to as consumer protection. The various provisions in this area have been discussed in the House today and when the previous bill was debated on second reading in March of this year. Briefly speaking, these provisions cover the subjects of misleading advertising, bait and switch selling, pyramid selling, referral selling, the professional sports provisions, and resale price maintenance to an extent. At the moment, most of these are still within the criminal law framework; they are in the form of prohibitions to violations to which penalties will attach.
These various subjects were discussed at great length at the Special Committee on Trends in Food Prices. It was one of the recommendations of that special committee that these aspects of the earlier competition bill be brought forward at the earliest opportunity, and I assume that the re-introduction of this bill is in response to a general feeling in the country that these undesirable trade practices require regulation.
It is generally the position of our party that those provisions, with a few technical exceptions, are desirable and should be expeditiously enacted into law in this way to assist the consumer who, at this time, is confronted by the ravages of a runaway inflation and spiralling cost of living, and therefore is in need of any protective mechanisms which we as a parliament are in a position to supply.
On the other hand, this bill contains another whole area which creates a new civil jurisdiction in the form of a restrictive trade practices commission which will become, for all intents and purposes, a powerful new judicial or quasi-judicial tribunal. While replacing the criminal jurisdiction with civil jurisdiction in this area of the law is probably desirable, I think it will be acknowledged on both sides of the House that there are thereby created potential problems which pertain to the sweeping nature and extent of the powers to be given to the restrictive trade practices commission by the legislation before us. To a certain extent the power given to the commission is discretionary and, to a certain extent, it is power given to a tribunal in this country which may fairly be said to be unprecedented.
Despite disclaimers to the contrary there are problems about the scope and the extent of a so-called right of appeal from this tribunal which may continue to cause considerable concern to a great many people.
There are also problems relating to the procedures to be followed by that tribunal. The bill before us refers to certain practices which will be subject to review by the restrictive trade practices commission, practices which the government has itself acknowledged may in some circumstances be desirable, which may be permitted by the commission and, in other situations and other circumstances, may be considered undesirable and subject to a prohibitive order of that tribunal. The powers of the commission in this respect are civil and discretionary in their application.
October 22, 1974

The bill before us involves fundamental philosophical considerations of a political, legal, economic and federal-provincial nature. To all intents and purposes it creates a new, highly centralized agency which has the potential of interposing itself into a major segment of Canadian political and economic life. Affecting matters within both federal and provincial jurisdiction, the legislation will permit the restrictive trade practices commission to alter or restructure market distribution systems in Canada in an unprecedented fashion.
This is major legislation and deserves careful scrutiny and a full and informed debate, not only by members of this House but by the many consumer groups, business interests and provincial governments who will be directly affected by its provisions.
By this legislation a restrictive trade practices commission has had effectively delegated to it the power to make decisions which can have a fundamental policy impact on relations between sovereign countries, and which could adversely affect Canada's foreign trade or external relations. By so doing the government will be abdicating its own responsibilities to make policy decisions of this magnitude.
I strongly urge that the government reconsider delegating in this way decision-making power of this magnitude to the commission, and consider vesting it in the governor-in-council, in the same fashion that it does in making decisions to reduce tariffs or in making decisions respecting the so-called "significant benefit" provision under the Foreign Investment Review Act.
The powers of the restrictive trade practices commission in this area should be limited to making recommendations to cabinet, but let us not have any abdication of responsibility on fundamental questions of economic policy. The Canadian public are entitled to know what the government of Canada will do about the implementation of a foreign law that may affect our external trade or foreign relations. This responsibility is appropriately the government's and it ought not to shift this responsibility to a commission such as the restrictive trade practices commission.
The point, Mr. Speaker, is not who is right or wrong in a particular case. The issue is who should be the responsible body for conducting our affairs with other countries with whom our trade and investment connections provide an infinite series of effects and counter-effects vis-a-vis each other. It is truly an astounding proposal that a responsible government would see fit to turn over in this way, even on a limited basis, such power to an appointed, independent body having no general responsibility for the conduct of relations between Canada and other countries.
Let us now turn to a review of some of the powers which it is proposed will be granted to the restrictive trade practices commission. Take first the far-reaching power to review instances of refusals to sell a product and to order a supplier to supply or to recommend tariff changes.
The implementation of this power may have a radical impact on the nature of distribution systems for products in Canada totally inconsistent with the real economic and structural facts of life in this country. The provision puts
Combines Investigation Act
the onus on the seller to justify his distribution system when he is called before the commission. Why not follow the ordinary principles inherent in our judicial system in this country, and place the onus on the director of investigation and research who brings the initial application to establish at least a prima facie case of inadequate competition?
It is simply not true to say that in all cases or even in most cases a refusal to sell is equivalent to inadequate competition; however, the temptation to draw this conclusion for the commission could lead to serious abuses. This provision raises serious questions and has serious implications for various franchise systems, the practice of private branding, off-shore suppliers and technical servicing requirements.
This criticism applies equally to the exclusive agency and tied sales provisions. Today a manufacturer can sign an agreement with a distributor requiring the distributor to promote and sell only his products. To both parties the common business sense of this is obvious. The seller gets a distributor with a strong interest in promoting his products. The distributor is ensured his efforts will not be expropriated by someone else.
If the commission gets under way, however, by defining a product restrictively it could, in the case of a car dealership, for example, result in a Volkswagen dealer getting an order allowing him to break his contracts of exclusivity and, at the same time, an order against Toyota and General Motors requiring them to supply him with cars. The result would be bad for the three manufacturers because of decreased sales efforts, bad for the consumer because of the dealer's probable inability to service three makes of cars, and no doubt eventually bad for the other dealers, one, or more, or all of whom could very well end up going out of business.
The net result would be less competition, not more, even though there might appear to be a short-term benefit. I would have hoped that the minister would provide a fuller explanation of what he is trying to achieve and how he justifies the means that he has adopted.
I also suggest to the minister that there are procedural problems and questions which must be raised in connection with the powers that are to be granted to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. To leave a commission of this sort free to make its own rules for the regulation of its proceedings and the performance of its duties and functions may well lead to uncertainty and arbitrariness in proceedings before the commission, problems which could easily be overcome through specifying certain minimum procedural protections in the legislation itself.
The act should spell out in relation to persons who might be called before the commission the right to reasonable notice of the hearing, the right to call and examine witnesses and to cross-examine other witnesses, the right to reasonable adjournments of the hearing and, finally and perhaps most important, the right to a written decision with reasons. I suggest further that the minister should consider carefully whether there is a need for a substantive right of appeal to the courts from an order of the restrictive trade practices commission.

October 22, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
I am instinctively suspicious and skeptical when it is explained to me that a right of appeal on the merits is denied Canadians on the grounds that the decision-making tribunal possesses special expertise or sophistication which has been denied to or is lacking in the judiciary of this country. That explanation is sheer nonsense. The members of our judiciary are trained and competent to hear and determine on appeal questions of law and fact determined by any quasi judicial or judicial tribunal in this country, however complex may be the facts and issues involved.
It must simply be made incumbent upon the restrictive trade practices commission to articulate clearly and precisely in written form the factual situation and the law applied to the factual situation by it in arriving at its conclusions affecting the rights of Canadians.
Returning to the consumer protection provisions dealing with such matters as misleading advertising, bait and switch-selling, untrue or misleading warranties and pyramid selling, there are a few matters of principle which I would urge the minister to consider. Why, for example, has the government eliminated the defence of honest mistake under those sections? In moving from the credulous man test to the general impression test, why did the government consider it necessary to propose in new section 36(5) to insert a literal meaning test as well? Why does the government exempt printers and publishers from misleading advertising prosecutions but not broadcasters?
To what extent, if at all, has there been consultation with provincial governments which possess jurisdiction to introduce their own legislation on warranties and testimonials and the other objectionable practices mentioned? What potential for conflict with provincial legislation exists in the absence of consultation, thus causing uncertainty and confusion for those engaged in commercial activity? Or is this simply another example of the propensity of the government to substitute confrontation for consultation in its dealings and relations with the governments of the provinces of Canada.
In considering the far-reaching powers to be granted by this legislation to the restrictive trade practices commission, I reiterate the hope expressed by my former colleague, Ron Atkey, that all members of this House will ask themselves the question whether all the provisions of the legislation before us, affecting as they do in such a sweeping and arbitrary fashion the rights and freedoms of Canadians, are really necessary.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this piece of proposed legislation has a long history, as detailed by previous speakers. Originally it was introduced as Bill C-256. The minister of the day, who is now Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford), ran into heavy opposition from the business community and the bill never got off the ground. Then, after the election in 1972 and a change of ministers, we saw another approach to combines legislation under a new minister. We examined the legislation, then Bill C-227. That became, eventually, Bill C-7, and now we call it Bill C-2. Really, the only thing that has changed is the number on the face of the bill.
First we had the Economic Council of Canada study in 1966, then the clean sweep approach with Bill C-256, and its appropriate reintroduction in 1972. Next we had an election, and a new minister with the slightly different approach of breaking the proposed legislation into two or three pieces as in Bill C-227 and Bill C-7. That meant debate, hearings, committee meetings, and finally we had another election, another new minister, more press releases, more debates, more hearings and so and so forth.
I do not like to say this, Mr. Speaker, but I was not impressed with the minister in his previous portfolio. In view of his dismal performance as postmaster general I thought he would have taken a different approach to this bill, and either have tabled all the amendments he proposed, or have brought in an amended bill with the changes that arose from the previous meetings and briefs on this proposed legislation.
We have before us now for second reading Bill C-2 that is identical to Bills C-227 and C-7. And we have the minister's press statement that he has numerous amendments to present in committee. Why do we not have these before us now, Mr. Speaker? Why do we not have at least a list of the proposed amendments? The minister cannot say why he has not presented them. He certainly has had enough time and, with his vastly increased budget and staff, he should have the people and the resources to prepare an amended bill. His former cabinet colleague, the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), left behind a mountain of testimony and comment.
I wonder why the minister has chosen to bring in the same bill. Knowing the difficulties of combines legislation I would have thought he would have previewed for the business community the broad outline of the total objectives of the proposed competition legislation.
We have phase I before us, and the minister discussed a little of phase II with the press but he says it is a long way off-some time in 1975. Then, of course, we have the anti-profiteering bill which, according to what I read in the press, will have a few changes but the same general thrust as before.
All these bills or phases will be amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. I think the business community has a right to know where they are heading and what ground rules they will have to work with in the future. It is time we all knew where we are heading. We found, for instance, that some provisions of Bill C-7 were in conflict with the anti-profiteering provisions presented in Bill C-29. Both bills were amendments to the anti-combines legislation. In fact, Bill C-29 amended Bill C-7 before it had passed second reading.
I notice the minister is quoted as saying he does not intend amendments to the Combines Investigation Act to become the instrument of the government to fight inflation, and he regrets it was ever identified as that. We could go through the record of the twenty-ninth parliament and see that dozens of times hon. members and ministers referred to the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act as part of the government's anti-inflation measures.

October 22, 1974

In fact the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made several references to this during the twenty-ninth parliament, stating that the proposed changes were part of his antiinflation program. It is refreshing then for the minister to admit that he does not intend the anti-combines legislation to become the instrument of the government to fight inflation. I commend the minister for being frank.
The bill before us is a bit of a non entity in that it is a bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act. The minister has amendments to amend the amendments to the act. Will the amendments change the fundamental nature of the bill? I think we have a right to know, and that is why members on this side of the House have been asking the question. It is not good enough that we sit here and just wait for amendments in committee. We are concerned that the amendments may change the fundamental nature of the bill, and I think the business community should be informed of the full impact of the legislation.
We are concerned too about the imbalances in the bill, and there are several. We note the lack of appeal against the decisions of the restrictive trade practices commission through the provincial courts. We have concern that we will be giving to the commission the authority to regulate Canadian business under civil law, but with powers of criminal law to enforce those regulations with no right to appeal. We will want some pretty clear discussions and definitions when we get to committee stage.
Many concerns have been expressed over the "refusal to sell" provisions in the bill. The impact on existing distribution systems in Canada will be dramatic, to say the least, if the bill is passed without amendment. It is not an offence under the proposed bill to refuse to sell, but it is subject to review by the restrictive trade practices commission. This places a cloud over the heads of those people in the distribution chain. We will want to have very clear guidelines so that the business community may operate openly, without the question or threat of a government board or commission interfering in their commercial affairs, and the frustration of not having the right to appeal a decision of the commission to the courts.
Through this legislation the minister wants to blanket business with additional restrictions, but at the same time wants to exempt certain groups. Banks are generally exempted from the provisions in the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. We ask why, Mr. Speaker? Why should they not be covered in the competition legislation? We do not accept the premise that they can be covered adequately by the Inspector General for Banks, who has neither the staff nor the time for that. We do not feel that through this device we should build another bureaucracy to control the banks when there is already that framework within the combines bill.
We notice that the labour unions are exempt from this provision. I realize it is probably not a political thing to say now, but in Hamilton we have a situation where a union has blackballed an entertainment establishment to the point that the proprietor cannot hire live entertainers. This is not the appropriate place to discuss the matter I know, but should both parties not be covered under the law so that they can resolve or settle the matter? On one side the union has caused economic loss by blackballing or delisting the proprietor, and on the other side the proprie-
Combines Investigation Act
tor has obviously grieved the union local and the losers are the entertainers.
The new advertising provisions exempt the federal government itself and its agencies, many of which are in that business. Take, for example, the CNR. For several years the CNR has been transporting Canadians as passengers in baggage cars, yet they advertise on the Toronto to Windsor run "Go CNR and Arrive Happier". I submit that a person cannot sit on the floor of a baggage car and arrive happier, regardless of how short the trip might be. When I pursued this matter with the TH & B, which also transports passengers from Hamilton to Buffalo in baggage cars, I was told the railway companies only guarantee passage; they do not guarantee a seat. I say this is false advertising but as I read the bill before us the CNR, at least, would be exempt from action either under its provisions or under other existing legislation.
There are those in Canada who would question whether the advertising of Canada's savings bonds as "safe and secure" is entirely ethical when one considers the net loss in purchasing power of these bonds.
The same applies to the perpetual bonds which sell for 25 per cent of their face value and pay about 3 per cent interest on which bond holders pay tax. I question very seriously whether the government should advertise such bonds as "safe and secure". In my view, if we are to apply the advertising rule to the commercial world, we should apply it to government agencies as well.
I see, incidentally, the Olympic coins being marketed as belonging to a limited edition. The minister was on the committee which discussed this matter. He probably remembers the meeting-at which we sat until two o'clock in the morning before having a long, informal discussion outside the West Block with the then president of the treasury board, now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury).
When the coinage bill was before parliament, hon. members on the government side did not want a limit placed on the number of coins that could be minted. They wanted the issue to be wide open. But now-and this is somewhat ironic-they market the coins as being from "a limited edition by act of parliament". Yet it was only because of an amendment put forward by the official opposition, and accepted by the minister, that a limit was fixed. Even so, I suggest that $450 million worth of coins is hardly what comes to mind as being a limited edition. I might add, though, that I bought some of these coins and helped to sell them to my friends. So I do my bit for the Olympics.
I do not take issue with the basic principle of the bill. We want companies to operate in a market that is as free and competitive as possible. We want the consumer to enjoy a good selection of products at competitive prices and in price ranges to suit his need. We do not want to see the consumer misled or duped, or see him the victim of pyramid sales, or tied sales, or referral sales, or of any of the questionable practices adopted by persons who operate on the borderline of business ethics and morality. This portion of the bill I support, and I am sure everyone in our party supports the consumer side of the legislation.

October 22, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
But we point out that the bill embodies certain questionable limitations. By seeking to exempt the government's departments, banks, labour unions and marketing boards from its provisions, the bill would eliminate a great many people engaged in commercial activities who are in a position to abuse the consumer and create an imbalance in the commercial endeavours of the business community.
If we pass laws like this, they should apply to everyone. I cannot suggest too strongly that the minister should produce a paper, be it any colour he wishes, white, green or yellow, setting forth in clear language the aims of his department as they pertain to business.
The businessman is already confused, to say the least, by the ever-increasing intrusion of government into business. He must comply with a tax act which he cannot interpret. He is affected by tariff regulations which are constantly changing. He is inundated by demands for reports from various government departments. He is being asked to produce more, to increase supplies, to work harder to improve productivity, to pay more taxes, to try to beat inflation, and to contribute more toward unemployment insurance premiums while he finds it difficult to hire adequate staff. And now he sees a restrictive trade practices commission looming on the horizon, a body which will be independent of the government, a body which will have the power to make its own regulations and from whose rulings there will be no appeal.
If the minister really wants to help the small businessman in Canada, and consumers as well, he might ponder means by which we can prevent United States commercial interests from making agreements with offshore manufacturers to supply not only the American market but the Canadian market as well.
Over the years I have talked to hundreds of young business people who found that the distribution of an important product which is sold in Canada was tied up by a United States business concern. In the final analysis, the consumer usually pays more because there is another profit step to be taken into account.
There is the famous-or should I call it the infamous- case of Mr. Harry Dunnett of Burlington, a small businessman who distributed musical instruments. This man started his business from scratch and did quite well. Unfortunately for him, after a few months one of his major offshore suppliers would not sell him any more of his products. He was at a loss to know why. He had sold all the supplies he could get from that particular producer and had paid for all his orders in advance.
Eventually, he found that a United States company, a large public corporation, had approached his supplier and told him they wanted Mr. Dunnett's supply cut off and their wholly owned Canadian subsidiary appointed as the exclusive Canadian distributor. The American company threatened to reduce its purchases from the offshore firm if it did not stop selling to Mr. Dunnett's Canadian company and conform to their wishes.
Thus we see a small Canadian company forced to the wall by an American company and its Canadian subsidiary, and there is no action which can be taken under any of our laws to protect this Canadian businessman. There is

no protection offered either in the Combines Investigation Act or in Bill C-2 which we have before us.
Strange though it may appear, Mr. Dunnett finds he can take some action under the Sherman anti-trust laws in the United States and he is pursuing this course at the present time. I find it ironic, to say the least, that a Canadian businessman should have to resort to a United States law to protect his interests. I realize we cannot pass legislation in Canada which would take effect beyond our borders, but we have other very considerable powers which we could use to protect our businessman from acts such as have been experienced by Mr. Dunnett.
Government members often talk of giving this bill or that bill fast passage, yet at the same time the minister says that he wants to hear all the arguments, positions and ideas that may improve a bill. The fact that this bill has had several runs in this House is beside the point; it is a serious piece of legislation and deserves careful rather than hurried consideration.
We cannot experiment at this stage with the distribution system in this country as if it were an academic exercise. The cost of establishing a distribution system is considerable. The function of distribution, with its backup administration, is extremely sensitive. The establishment of a backup service organization, and the tools and merchandising required to make it part of the distribution system constitute another cost to the whole function of the marketplace.
Before we look into and beyond this matter of refusal to sell and the control and distribution of markets, we have to be sure that we completely understand the function of the after market distribution system in this country. I am sure hon. members know there are many places in Canada that will just not support too competitive a market. Take Newfoundland as an example. In many cases the market will only support one or two business concerns in this field of endeavour. Therefore, before we set in motion something that will offset that, we have to assess whether in the long run we are really servicing that market and doing the consumers there any service or justice at all.
That about concludes my remarks, Mr. Speaker. I am looking forward to seeing the bill go to committee. I know that in committee we will give it long and serious discussion. I hope the minister and the members of the steering committee will not endeavour to restrict debate in any way, or hinder us from bringing before the committee witnesses who wish to appear. There were many who would have liked to appear before the standing committee of the twenty-ninth parliament but were not able to do so. Therefore I hope the minister will be broad enough in his outlook toward the legislation to see that we are able to receive these various people and hear their stories. We must ensure that the legislation we finally frame and pass through the House will not work hardship or inequity, but will in fact serve the business community and consumer, to the benefit of both.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME- CANADIAN POSITION ON A SECURE WORLD FOOD SYSTEM
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME- CANADIAN POSITION ON A SECURE WORLD FOOD SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a headline in the New York Times reads: "32 Nations Close to Starvation". Here are some of them: Bangladesh, India, Niger, Pakistan, Sudan, Upper Volta. All told, 700 million people live in these 32 countries. The countries are so poor and so short of food that crop failures and the high prices of grain, fertilizer and petroleum threaten them with bankruptcy, and their people with starvation.
The modern world has never faced a disaster of this magnitude. That is why the United Nations is sponsoring a world food conference in Rome. The conference opens two weeks from today. What role will Canada, a breadbasket of the world, play? No one knows.
I asked for a day's debate in parliament to focus attention on this global problem and on Canada's contribution to its solution. The government said no. Yesterday, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) proposed a motion calling on Canada to take the lead in establishing a world commission with the power to transfer food and resources where needed. This is the kind of structural solution the crisis demands. Responding for the government, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Corriveau) thought up all the reasons why this would not work, and then said that "a lot more aspects must be taken into consideration before we could be prepared to set up a concrete world food program."
In the name of God, Mr. Speaker, when will the government get off its fat, Canadian ass and recognize our responsibility to a starving world? How many more television pictures of emaciated children do we have to look at before the government will provide some leadership? How much longer will we enjoy the luxury of worrying about meat prices when millions cannot even get bread?
Two weeks ago representatives from non-governmental organizations from across Canada assembled in Ottawa for the Canadian conference on the world food crisis. I urged the delegates to formulate strong recommendations to the Canadian government that would force Canada to go beyond a mere philanthropic approach at the world food conference, because more dollars for food aid will not be enough. The conference passed a series of visionary and constructive recommendations that deal both with the immediate food emergency and the longer term structural causes of hunger and malnutrition.
I want to hear the government's response to the recommendations of the Canadian conference in a number of critical areas: first, guaranteeing that the developing countries themselves become as self-reliant as possible in food

October 22, 1974
Adjournment Debate
production-this is the only long-term solution to the food crisis; and second, immediate action to increase food production in Canada to meet the present emergency.
I was encouraged by the recent statement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to the effect that Canada could increase food production by 50 per cent in five years as long as farmers have guarantees that they will not be penalized for producing surpluses. I agree with him that Canadian farmers must not be forced to bear the whole burden of making more concessional sales of wheat and other foods to developing countries. But let us not deceive ourselves. A program of increased production aimed at making more food available at less cost to developing countries while subsidizing Canadian farmers will be much more costly than traditional food aid programs that dealt with unplanned agricultural surpluses.
One means of financing such a program would be the special tax on industrial raw material exports suggested by the conference. Another means would be to have the international community take on more responsibility for financing world food aid. This goal could be achieved either through an expanded role for the world food program, or through a new World Food Authority that would be established by the Rome conference. It is only just that developed nations which are net food importers, and particularly the petroleum exporting countries, should pay their fair share to whatever international authority is designated as having chief responsibility for world food aid.
One particularly visionary resolution of the Canadian Conference on the World Food Crisis proposes that a form of international taxation, based on ability to pay as measured by per capita income, be instituted to finance a world food plan. Under such a plan, Canadian taxpayers would pay their fair share, but would not be expected to bear the whole burden of producing agricultural surpluses for concessional sale to developing nations.
Canada has already indicated support for the proposal put forward by the Dr. Boerma of the U.N. Food and Agricultural Organization for international coordination of national grain stockpiles. This is a welcome first step, but it hardly fulfills the need for a truly international food bank.
Since it appears that it will not be politically feasible to establish a large grain reserve under international control at the Rome conference, cannot Canada at least take leadership in calling for a smaller international stockpile of food for emergency purposes?
The World Food Conference secretariat's plan of action recommends that such an emergency stockpile contain
500,000	tons of food which, in my opinion, is surely a minimum. Such a food bank for emergency relief could be stored in the developing world where it is most needed; it could be administered under international control with the participation of the developing countries themselves; and, most important, it could function to remove the temptation for food exporting nations to use their food surpluses for political purposes.
Third, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Conference on the World Food Crisis called for Canada to support the establishment of the new international economic order called

for by the sixth special session of the United Nations General Assembly last April and May. At the World Population Conference in Bucharest, which I attended, the Canadian delegation avoided making any commitment to the establishment of the new international economic order, despite the insistence of the developing nations and of many expert observers that the implementation of a new economic order is an essential precondition for effective action toward reducing the rate of population growth. Will Canada take the same position at the World Food Conference where the issue of the world economic order is even more crucial?
The growing imbalance in the distribution of wealth that is generated by the present world economic order is at the heart of the food crisis. In fact, last week Dr. Neal Stoskopf of the University of Guelph pointed out that instead of helping the have-not nations, the affluent nations actually import protein from protein-deficient countries.
The statement on "Sharing Daily Bread" issued by the Canadian Catholic Conference of Bishops points out that this scandalous and absurd situation is made possible because the distribution of food is governed by effective demand in the market place and not by human need.
Therefore any real solution of the food crisis must include a redistribution of wealth which determines effective demand, and any long term solution must enable developing countries to achieve greater patterns of selfsufficiency in food. Both of these goals are only possible under a new economic order.
Yet I have seen no evidence that the present government is willing to allow a fundamental restructuring of the world's economic system, a re-ordering of the allocation of food and raw materials, and the reforms of the international trade, monetary and financial institutions called for by the United Nations. Let us listen to Paul Gerin-Lajoie, Director of CIDA, who calls for a new enlightened Canadian attitude towards "a new international order which will help to reduce the present imbalance among nations." If ever there was a moment for Canada to give leadership in providing justice to a suffering humanity, that moment is now.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME- CANADIAN POSITION ON A SECURE WORLD FOOD SYSTEM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, after listening to the hon. member one is moved to paraphrase Cecil Rhodes: So much to say in so little time. I was impressed with the sincerity of the hon. member's remarks. Let me repeat, however, the assurance that Canada's position will not be restricted to emergency action, but will encompass and, indeed, put more emphasis on proposed structural changes in the world food system.
I should like to repeat the assurance that Canada's position will not be restricted to emergency action but will encompass, and indeed put great emphasis on proposed structural changes in the world food system. Several possibilities are now being studied. These include: diverting more Canadian aid into agricultural development in developing countries, provided developing countries are willing, where necessary, to reorder their priorities in favour of agricultural development; encouraging developed countries and other new holders of wealth to channel
October 22, 1974

increased amounts of aid into agricultural development in developing countries; and studying other long term options in the appropriate form, for example, liberalization of trade in agricultural goods.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-POSITION OF CANADA ON PARTICIPATION OF PALESTINIAN LIBERATION ORGANIZATION IN UNITED NATIONS DEBATE ON MIDDLE EAST
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-POSITION OF CANADA ON PARTICIPATION OF PALESTINIAN LIBERATION ORGANIZATION IN UNITED NATIONS DEBATE ON MIDDLE EAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the admission of the Palestinian Liberation Organization to the United Nations by an overwhelming vote of 105 for admission, four against admission, and twenty abstentions, I find I need a new reason to believe in the United Nations.
I know the United Nations well. At the beginning of my political career I spent three months there as a delegate. I understand how it works. In view of this and some other decisions on the Middle East problems, I wonder what justification and grounds there are now for reasonable men and men of peace to support that organization.
The Palestinian Liberation Organization has credentials to speak at the United Nations. It is not a government; it is not recognized by all Arab states; it is not even recognized by all the Palestinians. But it has credentials and I wish to read some of them. I have 20 events to recite. I do not know whether or not they were committed by the Palestinian Liberation Organization but it claims credit for them all.
This organization claims credit for these 20 events: hijacking of a civilian airline in 1970, bomb outrages in Jerusalem, bombing incidents in Tel-Aviv, an attack on an Israeli airplane in Athens, an attack on an Israeli airliner in Zurich, and diversion of a United States plane enroute to Israel. I do not wish to take the time of the House to go through the whole list. It is available. These things are documented. They are all things for which this organization claims credit, this organization which now heads for the United Nations with recognized status to speak. Let me refer to one item, number 18 on my list:
Arab terrorists' massacre of Israeli children at Maalot.
I have a newspaper clipping here from the Associated Press and Reuters about that incident. It states:
A Palestinian guerrilla leader said yesterday that the guerrilla attack on the town was "heroic" and warned that similar operations would be launched in the future.
Adjournment Debate
Later the article continues:
We promise the Palestinian people to undertake more such operations as they express a real sacrifice and represent the start of a new stage in the development of commando operations both in size and level.
Look who is coming to dinner; look who is coming to the United Nations. It is a terrorist gang whose objective is not only to establish a homeland for their own people but the total obliteration of the state of Israel. This is their stated objective.
There is nothing inevitable about the survival of state of Israel. That state can go at any time. We should remember that in this House. Canada is one of its friends, one of its best friends. We are committed to its survival. What I should like to say, now that this decision has been taken, not with Canada's approval but by an overwhelming majority of the members of the United Nations without Canada, is that Canada must make every effort to get the Palestinian Liberation Organization to clean up its acts, to denounce acts of terrorism, and to find a new way to put its case forward.
Above all, the PLO must grow to accept the right of the state of Israel to exist, and everything that goes with that right. If it cannot do that, if the PLO maintains its terrorist outlook, Israel may survive anyway. One thing that is obvious is that the survival of Israel does not depend on the United Nations.
But what about the United Nations? Its survival is not inevitable either, and I submit that the kind of decision that the UN took in admitting the PLO raises questions about whether that organization will survive.

Madam Speaker, the position of the government on this issue remains as outlined by the minister in reply to the hon. member on October 18. I note in his question the hon. member recognized that the decision taken by the UN was not with Canada's approval because at that time Canada abstained from the voting. I think his challenge is probably to the position that has been taken by the majority of UN members in that vote. Since the time of that vote, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) has had the opportunity to discuss this issue fully with the ambassador of Israel and the ambassadors of Arab countries resident in Ottawa, and they have expressed their full understanding of Canada's position.
The hon. member has indicated that surely the PLO should be able to find, rather than the violence which we have seen, a new way to put their case forward. It seems to me that perhaps this is a better way.

subtopic: HOUSING-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS FOR ASSISTED HOME OWNERSHIP PROGRAM-AVERAGE EFFECTIVE RATE OF INTEREST ON MORTGAGES-POSSIBLE SHIFT IN POLICY
HOUSING-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS FOR ASSISTED HOME OWNERSHIP PROGRAM-AVERAGE EFFECTIVE RATE OF INTEREST ON MORTGAGES-POSSIBLE SHIFT IN POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question which I asked the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) on October 15 had to do with whether the government proposed to increase the amount of funds made available through programs such as the

October 22, 1974
Adjournment Debate
Assisted Home Ownership Program and other programs, which would go some way at least to meeting the needs of the people in low and middle income brackets for housing which they are at present virtually unable to find at a price which they can afford to pay.
The number of housing starts this year is down substantially from what it was last year when there were 268,000 housing starts. This year there has been a drop of 25 per cent, and it has now been calculated that, unless there is a further deterioration in housing starts, we will build just over 200,000 units a year.
When I asked the question the other day, the minister replied by saying that the government had more than met the proposals made by the Economic Council of Canada some years ago that we build about 200,000 units a year. What the Economic Council said at that time was that we needed a minimum of 200,000 a year. It also argued that housing should not be used as a tool for manipulation, and yet that is precisely what has happened.
This year we are building fewer houses than we did last year, not because the people of Canada need fewer houses but because interest rates have gone well over 11 per cent and most people, including those in the middle income bracket, cannot afford to buy homes.
The minister said the fact that AHOP money has been used up is proof of the success of the program and that the need has been met. Madam Speaker, nothing could be further from the truth. From the beginning the money made available under AHOP was far less than the amount needed. The government, through Central Mortgage and Housing, cannot in this minuscule way meet the housing needs of the people of Canada.
Home ownership is not the answer for a substantial proportion of our people. The greatest need is in the area of housing accommodation for rent. This would be true even if sufficient money were made available under AHOP. As I say, we need a substantial increase in the stock of houses for rent, of which we build too few. We need subsidies for families who cannot afford to pay the market price of housing they must rent or own. In the 1940s all the Scandinavian countries realized this fact and adopted housing programs under which they provided houses for people who did not earn enough to buy their own.
In Canada we have done just the reverse. We have built houses, not because the Canadian people needed them, but because building them was necessary to overcome unemployment. Of course, with our present high interest rates, people cannot afford houses. Nevertheless, when unemployment is high, the government pumps money into the, housing field. When unemployment is low, we turn the tap off and stop money for housing.
If there is to be a stable vacancy rate and a stable housing program, we shall need a stable housing policy. I suggest that we need a government policy which will meet the housing needs of the people of Canada, and I include both those who buy and rent accommodation. We need houses that will meet the needs of the people of Canada; they should not be built merely to meet the goals of the government, that is, to reduce unemployment which may arise in the winter of 1974-75, the summer of 1975 or the

winter of 1975-76. Unemployment is one thing; the housing requirements of the Canadian people are another.
In every city of Canada-Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver and Winnipeg-we see the core deteriorating from year to year. We see more and more people forced into poor, dilapidated housing which is a disgrace to a country which has the manpower, lumber, copper and all those things one needs to build decent housing.
We have made a start. We have begun to meet the needs of senior citizens for adequate housing. I call on the minister to develop a program which will meet the housing needs of all people in Canada, regardless of income, and provide us with the sort of housing to which this affluent country is entitled.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: HOUSING-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS FOR ASSISTED HOME OWNERSHIP PROGRAM-AVERAGE EFFECTIVE RATE OF INTEREST ON MORTGAGES-POSSIBLE SHIFT IN POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, all Canadians can be proud of the fact that year in year out we have managed to build housing at a rythm that has surpassed that of the establishment of new families and immigration. During this period, we have markedly reduced overcrowding and improved housing for a good number of Canadians across the country.
This is greatly due to the Canadian building industry which magnificently met the programs elaborated by the federal government such as, for example, the Assisted Home-Ownership Program.
During the last six years, one of the main concerns of the federal government was to divide housing in a way that would allow low income families to share improved housing conditions with better off Canadians. The government therefore tried to reserve amounts at its disposal to provide first of all for housing for low or middle income families.
We have supported the provinces by granting loans and contributions for social housing. We have supported nonprofit groups who were building housing as well as nonprofit co-operative groups through starting-off funds, 100 per cent financing and 10 per cent contribution of investments to help produce housing for low income people. I have already mentioned the remarkable success of the Assisted Home-Ownership Program in which the government invested some $450 million since the beginning of this year.
It is this unique Canadian approach of partnership between the private sector and the public sector that has enabled us in recent years to attain such a high level of housing production. A target of one million houses over a five-year period was set by the Economic Council of Canada. The government made a commitment to reaching this goal back in 1969. We have surpassed this target, and I think it is to the credit of the housebuilding industry, and all governments concerned, that a total of 1,152,600 units have been produced in the five years.
We hope to continue to improve our programs in 1975. While there has been a drop in starts in recent months due to a variety of reasons including, for example, high mortgage interest rates and increases in the cost of labour and

materials, not to mention the cost of land, I am confident that the declining trend can be halted in 1975.
My minister does not propose at this time to set any precise figure for starts in 1975, but I can assure the House that the government has given careful consideration to the
Adjournment Debate
housing situation in Canada. We have carefully studied the prospects for next year, and we will take appropriate action to ensure a continuation in the general improvement of housing conditions for all Canadians.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.25 p.m.
